title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: ## Overview A Beacon is an alert rule attached to a metric. When the rule's condition is met, Kestrel sends a notification to one or more destinations. Beacons are the mechanism by which teams learn about a broken checkout, a spike in errors, or an unusually quiet signup flow without watching a dashboard. This specification reflects release 4.1, which added PagerDuty as a destination. ## What can be monitored A Beacon watches a single metric series. The series may be an event count (for example, `checkout_completed` per hour), a unique-user count, a property aggregate (sum or average of `cart_value`), a funnel conversion rate between two steps, or the size of a cohort. Filters and a single breakdown property are supported; when a breakdown is used, the Beacon evaluates each breakdown value independently and can fire for one value without firing for the others. ## Evaluation schedule

title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: Every Beacon in every project is evaluated every 5 minutes on a shared scheduler. Each evaluation looks at the most recently completed bucket of the metric's granularity, which may be 5 minutes, 1 hour, or 1 day. Because ingest visibility lag is usually under 30 seconds, a 5-minute bucket is normally complete by the time it is evaluated; for customers with unusually late-arriving mobile events we recommend hourly granularity. Following the 2026-02-19 incident, in which alerts were delayed by up to 47 minutes because of clock skew on the scheduler nodes, release 4.1.1 moved the scheduler to a monotonic clock and added catch-up evaluation for any window that was skipped. ## Condition modes Three modes are available. Threshold mode fires when the metric is above or below a fixed number. It is the simplest mode and needs no history.

title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: It is the simplest mode and needs no history. Percent change mode, added in release 3.5, fires when the metric moves by more than a configured percentage compared with the same bucket in a previous period. The comparison period may be the previous bucket, the same bucket one day earlier, or the same bucket one week earlier. The week-earlier comparison is the usual choice for metrics with a strong weekly cycle. Anomaly mode, added in release 4.0, fits a seasonal baseline with daily and weekly components and fires when the observed value falls outside the expected band. Anomaly mode requires at least 14 days of history for the metric; a Beacon created in anomaly mode on a younger metric stays in a "warming up" state and does not fire until the history requirement is met. The sensitivity setting controls the width of the band. ## Destinations

title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: A Beacon can notify up to four destinations at once: Slack (via an incoming webhook or the Kestrel Slack app), PagerDuty (Events API v2, added in 4.1), a generic webhook that receives a signed JSON payload, and email. Webhook payloads are signed with an HMAC using a per-project secret so that receivers can verify authenticity. Failed deliveries are retried three times over 15 minutes and then logged in the project's audit log on Growth and Scale plans. ## Firing, recovery, and cooldown When a condition is met the Beacon fires and enters a cooldown, during which repeated breaches do not send further notifications. The default cooldown is 30 minutes and can be set between 5 minutes and 24 hours. A recovery notification is sent when the condition has been clear for two consecutive evaluations. Muting a Beacon pauses notifications but not evaluation, so its history remains complete. ## Limits by plan

title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: The number of Beacons a project may hold depends on its plan: Starter projects may create 5 Beacons, Growth projects 60, and Scale projects 500. All three condition modes and all four destination types are available on every plan; the plan limit is purely on count. A Beacon that uses a breakdown counts as one Beacon regardless of how many breakdown values it produces. Projects at their limit must delete or merge Beacons before creating new ones; the Plans and Limits document lists the caps alongside the other plan differences. ## Relationship to cohorts and funnels Cohort-size Beacons are the most common pattern for retention monitoring: a behavioural cohort such as "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" (see Funnels and Cohorts Specification) paired with a percent change Beacon gives an early signal of checkout problems.

title: Beacons: Alerting Specification
text: Cohort-size Beacons are the most common pattern for retention monitoring: a behavioural cohort such as "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" (see Funnels and Cohorts Specification) paired with a percent change Beacon gives an early signal of checkout problems. Because behavioural cohorts are recomputed hourly, a cohort-size Beacon should use hourly granularity to avoid evaluating a stale value several times in a row. ## Example Acme Retail runs a threshold Beacon on `error_payment_declined` per 5 minutes with a threshold of 40, notifying Slack and PagerDuty, and an anomaly Beacon on unique users performing `checkout_completed` per hour notifying Slack only. The first catches gateway outages within minutes; the second catches the quieter failure where checkouts silently drop without producing errors.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: ## Overview Funnels and cohorts are the two core analysis primitives in Kestrel. A funnel measures how users move through an ordered sequence of events; a cohort is a named set of users defined either by behaviour or by an uploaded list. Both are available on every plan, including Starter, and both are computed by the Osprey query engine introduced in Kestrel 4.0. This document reflects the behaviour as of release 4.1. ## Funnel definition A funnel consists of between 2 and 12 steps. Each step is an event name, optionally filtered by property conditions such as `country = 'DE'` or `cart_value > 100`. The first step defines the population entering the funnel; every subsequent step is measured as the share of users from the previous step who performed it within the conversion window. The conversion window can be set anywhere from 1 minute to 90 days and is measured from the timestamp of the first step for each user, not from the previous step.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: The conversion window can be set anywhere from 1 minute to 90 days and is measured from the timestamp of the first step for each user, not from the previous step. A user who completes step one on Monday and step four on the following Monday with a 7-day window is counted as converted; a user who takes eight days is not, even if each individual gap was short. ## Strict versus loose ordering Since release 4.1 a funnel can be evaluated in one of two ordering modes. In strict ordering, the default and the only mode available before 4.1, a user must perform the steps in exactly the configured sequence with no other funnel steps in between; performing step three before step two resets the user to the last completed step. In loose ordering, steps must still occur in sequence but other events, including other steps performed out of order, do not reset progress.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: In loose ordering, steps must still occur in sequence but other events, including other steps performed out of order, do not reset progress. Loose ordering is generally the right choice for onboarding flows where users wander, and strict ordering for checkout flows where the sequence is enforced by the product itself. ## Breakdowns A funnel can be broken down by up to 3 properties at once, producing one conversion series per combination. This limit was raised from 2 to 3 in release 3.4. Breakdown values with fewer than 20 users in the first step are grouped into an "Other" bucket to keep charts readable; this grouping can be disabled per funnel but the cap of 3 properties cannot be raised. Each breakdown property may be an event property, a user property, or a cohort membership flag. ## Time-to-convert For every step transition the funnel view shows median, p75, and p90 time to convert. These are computed over converted users only.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: These are computed over converted users only. Exporting the funnel to CSV includes the per-step counts, conversion rates, and the three timing percentiles; per-user exports are available through KQL instead (see SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference). ## Behavioural cohorts A behavioural cohort is defined by a rule such as "performed `checkout_completed` at least 2 times in the last 30 days and has not performed `subscription_cancelled`". Rules may combine up to 8 conditions with AND and OR. Behavioural cohorts are recomputed every hour; the recomputation for all cohorts in a project runs as a single job, so a project with many complex cohorts may see its membership lag the top of the hour by several minutes. Events flagged `late=true` by the ingest layer are not included in hourly recomputation and are picked up by the nightly full pass instead. ## Static cohorts A static cohort is created by uploading a CSV of `distinct_id` values.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: A static cohort is created by uploading a CSV of `distinct_id` values. Static cohort upload was introduced in release 3.4. A single upload may contain at most 250,000 user IDs; larger lists must be split into several cohorts. IDs that do not match a known user are stored anyway and become active when a matching user first appears, which makes static cohorts useful for pre-loading marketing lists ahead of a campaign. Static cohorts never change unless re-uploaded. ## Limits A project may hold at most 200 cohorts across both kinds. Deleted cohorts count against this limit for 24 hours while the deletion propagates to Warehouse Sync (see Warehouse Sync Specification) and Beacons. A cohort can be referenced by any number of funnels, Beacons, and syncs, so the practical advice is to create a small number of reusable cohorts rather than one per report. ## Interaction with plans Funnel and cohort features do not vary by plan.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: Funnel and cohort features do not vary by plan. What does vary is the retention window over which they can be evaluated: 30 days on Starter, 13 months on Growth, and 25 months on Scale. A funnel with a 90-day conversion window on a Starter project will therefore only ever see users whose first step is within the last 30 days, and the interface warns about this when the window exceeds retention. The Plans and Limits document has the full comparison. ## Worked example Acme Retail defines a four-step checkout funnel: `product_viewed`, `add_to_cart`, `checkout_started`, `checkout_completed`, with a 3-day window and strict ordering, broken down by `device_type` and `country`. They pair it with a behavioural cohort "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" (performed `checkout_started` but not `checkout_completed`) and attach a Beacon that fires when the cohort grows by more than 15 percent versus the previous day.

title: Funnels and Cohorts Specification
text: They pair it with a behavioural cohort "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" (performed `checkout_started` but not `checkout_completed`) and attach a Beacon that fires when the cohort grows by more than 15 percent versus the previous day. That combination of funnel, cohort, and Beacon is the pattern most teams converge on.

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: ## Purpose The Event Ingestion API is the single entry point for all event data flowing into Kestrel. Every SDK, server-side integration, and third-party connector ultimately calls this endpoint. This specification describes the v2 contract as shipped in Kestrel 4.0. The legacy `/v1/ingest` endpoint, deprecated since 3.4, was removed in 4.0 and now returns HTTP 410 Gone. ## Endpoint and request shape Events are sent with `POST /v2/ingest` to the regional base URL of the project. US projects use the Oregon endpoint and EU projects use the Frankfurt endpoint; the region is fixed at project creation and cannot be changed afterwards, so integrations should read the region from project settings rather than hard-coding it. A request body is a JSON object with a single `events` array. A batch may contain at most 500 events and the encoded body may not exceed 2 MB, whichever is reached first.

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: A batch may contain at most 500 events and the encoded body may not exceed 2 MB, whichever is reached first. Requests that exceed either bound are rejected with HTTP 413 and the whole batch is discarded, so clients must split rather than retry as-is. Each event carries a `name`, a `timestamp` in RFC 3339, a `distinct_id`, an optional `event_id`, and a `properties` object. An event may hold at most 120 properties, and any single property value may be at most 4 KB after serialisation. Oversized properties are truncated and the event is flagged with `truncated=true` rather than rejected. Authentication uses a project write key in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. Write keys are scoped to a single project and region. ## Response codes A successful request returns HTTP 202 Accepted.

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: A successful request returns HTTP 202 Accepted. Note that 202 means the batch was durably written to the ingest queue, not that it is already queryable; the typical delay between acceptance and visibility in funnels is under 30 seconds. See the Ingest Pipeline Architecture document for the path an event takes after acceptance. When a project exceeds its rate limit the API returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header expressed in seconds. Clients are expected to honour that header with bounded exponential backoff. The official SDKs (see SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference) do this automatically and buffer events locally in the meantime. Malformed JSON returns HTTP 400 with a per-event error list. A batch containing some valid and some invalid events is accepted partially: valid events are queued, invalid ones are listed in the response under `rejected` with their index. ## Rate limits by plan

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: Rate limits are enforced per project, not per write key, and are measured in requests per second rather than events per second. Starter projects are limited to 350 requests per second. This figure was raised from 200 in release 3.5 after telemetry showed that mobile SDK batching was producing short bursts that tripped the older limit. Growth projects are limited to 1,800 requests per second, and Scale projects to 7,500 requests per second. Customers who need more on Scale can request a temporary uplift through their customer success manager. Because a single request can carry up to 500 events, even a Starter project can theoretically ingest 175,000 events per second in short bursts. In practice the monthly event allowance of the plan (2,000,000 events on Starter, 25,000,000 on Growth, and 250,000,000 or more on Scale) is the binding constraint for most customers; overage pricing is described in the Plans and Limits document.

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: In practice the monthly event allowance of the plan (2,000,000 events on Starter, 25,000,000 on Growth, and 250,000,000 or more on Scale) is the binding constraint for most customers; overage pricing is described in the Plans and Limits document. ## Idempotency and deduplication Each event should carry an `event_id`. We recommend UUIDv7 because its time-ordered prefix keeps the deduplication index compact. If two events arrive with the same `event_id` within the project's retention window, the second is silently dropped and the response still returns 202. Events without an `event_id` are assigned one on arrival and therefore cannot be deduplicated by the client; this is acceptable for fire-and-forget page views but not for billing or checkout events. ## Late and backdated events Kestrel accepts events whose timestamp is in the past.

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text:
Kestrel accepts events whose timestamp is in the past. Events older than 72 hours at the time of arrival are still stored but are flagged `late=true`, and hourly cohort recomputation does not pick them up until the next full nightly pass. Events with a timestamp more than 5 minutes in the future are clamped to the arrival time and flagged `clock_skew=true`. Backfilling a large history should be done in chronological order and at a steady rate rather than in one burst; the 429 handling described above will throttle the backfill safely. ## Sample request A minimal batch looks like this: POST /v2/ingest
   Authorization: Bearer kw_live_9f2c...
   {"events": [
     {"name": "checkout_completed",
      "timestamp": "2025-10-07T09:12:44Z",
      "distinct_id": "user_48213",
      "event_id": "0192c1e4-7a3b-7c1d-9b2f-3e4a5b6c7d8e",
      "properties": {"cart_value": 129.50, "currency": "USD", "country": "NL"}}
   ]} ## Operational notes

title: Event Ingestion API Specification
text: The ingest tier is horizontally scaled and stateless. During the 2025-07-14 incident (INC-2025-07) roughly 38 percent of requests in the US region received 503 responses for just over three hours; clients that retried with backoff lost no data, while clients that treated 503 as fatal lost events. This is the strongest argument for always using the official SDKs or implementing equivalent retry logic. Status page updates for ingest incidents follow the on-call process described in the On-Call Runbook.

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: ## SDK overview Kestrel ships five official SDKs: JavaScript (browser and Node.js), iOS (Swift), Android (Kotlin), Python, and Go. All five are open source, wrap the Event Ingestion API, and implement the same retry contract: on HTTP 429 they honour the `Retry-After` header with exponential backoff, on 5xx they retry up to five times, and in both cases they buffer events locally so that nothing is lost while waiting. The Go SDK reached general availability in release 3.4 and the Python SDK gained an async client in release 3.5. This document reflects release 4.1. ## JavaScript SDK The browser build auto-captures page views and clicks when initialised with `autocapture: true`. Auto-captured clicks record the element's tag, text, and CSS path, which is what powers rage-click moments in Trails. Form field values are never captured.

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: Form field values are never captured. Events are batched and flushed every 10 seconds or when 20 events accumulate, whichever comes first, and the SDK flushes on `visibilitychange` so that events are not lost when a tab is closed. The Node.js build has no auto-capture and is intended for server-side events such as order confirmations. ## Mobile SDKs The iOS and Android SDKs batch events and flush every 30 seconds or when 50 events accumulate. Both persist the queue to disk. The Android SDK gained an offline queue in release 3.6 that holds up to 10,000 events while the device has no connectivity and drains them in chronological order on reconnect; the iOS SDK has had the same behaviour since its initial release. Events sent after a long offline period may arrive more than 72 hours after their timestamp and will be flagged `late=true` by the ingest layer. ## Python and Go SDKs

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: The Python SDK offers a synchronous client and, since release 3.5, an async client built on `asyncio`. The Go SDK uses a background goroutine with a channel-based queue. Both are intended for backend services and data pipelines and default to a batch size of 100 events and a flush interval of 5 seconds. Both expose a `Flush()` call for use before process exit. ## Identity Every SDK exposes `identify(distinct_id, properties)` to attach a stable identity to the current device, and `alias(new_id, old_id)` to merge an anonymous pre-login identity into a known user. Aliasing is one-way and permanent. User properties set through `identify` are visible in Trails and usable as funnel breakdowns and cohort conditions. ## Kestrel Query Language KQL is a read-only, SQL-like language for querying events directly. It is available in the interface, through the Query API, and as the source for metric syncs in Warehouse Sync.

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: It is available in the interface, through the Query API, and as the source for metric syncs in Warehouse Sync. A query names a source, applies filters, sets a time range, and aggregates. The canonical example: EVENTS WHERE name = 'checkout' SINCE 7d COUNT BY country The `SINCE` shorthand, added in release 3.5, accepts durations such as `15m`, `6h`, `7d`, and `3mo`, as well as absolute timestamps. The older `BETWEEN` clause remains available for explicit ranges. Aggregations include `COUNT`, `COUNT UNIQUE distinct_id`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, and percentile functions `P50`, `P90`, `P99`. `BY` groups by one or more properties; `BUCKET 1h` groups by time. ## KQL limits A query returns at most 10,000 rows. Queries that would exceed this return the first 10,000 rows and set a `truncated` flag in the response; the correct remedy is a narrower filter or a coarser bucket.

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: Queries that would exceed this return the first 10,000 rows and set a `truncated` flag in the response; the correct remedy is a narrower filter or a coarser bucket. Every query has a 60-second timeout; this was raised from 30 seconds in release 4.1 after the Osprey engine made long-range queries over cold storage practical. Query API concurrency is limited per plan to 8 concurrent queries on Starter, 40 on Growth, and 160 on Scale; a request beyond the limit receives HTTP 429. Queries are served from the hot store for the last 7 days and from columnar cold storage for older data, so a query that spans the boundary may take noticeably longer than one that stays within the last week. Results are cached for 10 minutes, and identical queries within that window are served from cache and do not count against concurrency. ## Query API `POST /v2/query` accepts a JSON body with a `kql` string and returns rows as JSON.

title: SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference
text: `POST /v2/query` accepts a JSON body with a `kql` string and returns rows as JSON. It uses a project read key, which is distinct from the write key used for ingest. Read keys can be scoped to a single saved query for embedding in customer-facing dashboards. ## Choosing between KQL and the interface Funnels, cohorts, and Beacons are best built in the interface, which handles ordering logic, conversion windows, and evaluation schedules. KQL is the right tool for ad hoc questions, for exporting per-user data that the funnel CSV export does not include, and for feeding metric syncs. A common pattern is to prototype a metric in KQL, save it, attach a Beacon to it, and sync it to the warehouse, all from the same saved query.

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text: ## What Trails is Trails is Kestrel's per-user chronological timeline. Opening a Trail for a `distinct_id` shows every event that user generated, in order, with the properties attached to each one, grouped into sessions. It is the tool support and product teams use to answer "what exactly did this user do before they churned or filed a ticket". This specification describes Trails as of release 3.6, which introduced automatic moment detection. ## What Trails is not Trails is not session replay. Kestrel does not record the DOM, screenshots, mouse movement, or keystrokes, and the JavaScript SDK never captures form values. A Trail is reconstructed entirely from the events the customer chose to send. Teams evaluating Kestrel sometimes expect a video-like playback; the correct expectation is a structured, searchable event log with annotations.

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text: Teams evaluating Kestrel sometimes expect a video-like playback; the correct expectation is a structured, searchable event log with annotations. This design keeps the SDK payload small and avoids collecting personal data the customer never intended to send. ## Sessions Events are grouped into sessions using a 30-minute inactivity gap. The gap is measured on event timestamps, not arrival time, so late events (those flagged `late=true` by the Event Ingestion API) are slotted into the correct historical session once they arrive. A session that spans midnight is not split. Each session shows its duration, event count, entry event, and exit event. ## Moments Release 3.6 added automatic moment detection. A moment is a segment of a Trail that the system flags as likely interesting. Three moment types are detected:

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text:
Three moment types are detected: - Rage clicks: five or more click events on the same element within 3 seconds, captured by the JavaScript SDK's auto-capture.
- Dead ends: a session that ends within 10 seconds of a page view with no further interaction.
- Error bursts: three or more events named with the `error_` prefix within 60 seconds. Moments are shown as markers on the timeline and can be filtered in the Trails list view, so a support engineer can ask for "all users with an error burst in the last 24 hours". Moment detection runs on the enriched event stream (see Ingest Pipeline Architecture), so moments appear within a minute of the underlying events. ## Sampling Trails is a Growth and Scale feature; it is not available on Starter projects. On Growth, Trails are sampled at 25 percent of users, chosen deterministically by hashing the `distinct_id` so that a sampled user is sampled consistently over time.

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text: On Growth, Trails are sampled at 25 percent of users, chosen deterministically by hashing the `distinct_id` so that a sampled user is sampled consistently over time. On Scale, Trails are captured for 100 percent of users. Sampling applies only to the Trails view; the underlying events are always stored in full and remain available to funnels, cohorts, and KQL regardless of plan. ## Retention Trail retention is shorter than event retention. Growth projects keep Trails for 30 days and Scale projects for 90 days, after which the per-user timeline index is dropped even though the raw events remain queryable for the plan's event retention window (13 months on Growth, 25 months on Scale). This distinction matters when a customer asks why a user's events are visible in KQL but their Trail is empty: the events are older than the Trail retention window. ## Search and filters

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text: The Trails list can be filtered by cohort membership, by presence of a moment type, by any user property, and by an event performed in a time range. Searching by `distinct_id` or by any identifying user property such as email is exact-match only. Results are limited to 1,000 users per query; narrower filters should be used rather than paging through larger sets. ## Privacy controls Project admins can mark user properties as sensitive, in which case they are masked in Trails for members without the "view sensitive properties" permission. Deleting a user through the privacy deletion endpoint removes their Trail immediately and their events according to the Data Retention Policy. Trails respects the project's region, so EU-region projects have their Trail indexes in Frankfurt. ## Typical use Acme Retail's support team links their helpdesk to Kestrel so that every ticket carries a direct link to the customer's Trail.

title: Trails: User Timeline Specification
text: Acme Retail's support team links their helpdesk to Kestrel so that every ticket carries a direct link to the customer's Trail. When a ticket mentions a failed checkout, the engineer opens the Trail, jumps to the most recent error burst moment, and sees the `error_payment_declined` event with its `gateway_response` property, which usually resolves the ticket without involving engineering. Product teams use the rage click moment filter to build a weekly list of the most frustrating elements in the interface.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: ## Purpose Warehouse Sync is Kestrel's reverse-ETL feature. It pushes computed data — cohort memberships and metric results — out of Kestrel and into the customer's own data warehouse, where it can be joined with billing, CRM, and support data that never passes through Kestrel. The direction is always Kestrel to warehouse; Kestrel does not read from the customer's warehouse. This specification describes the feature as of release 4.1. ## Plan availability Warehouse Sync is available on Growth and Scale plans. It is not available on Starter. Growth projects can sync to Snowflake and BigQuery. Scale projects can additionally sync to Amazon Redshift, which was added as a destination in release 4.1. The destination list is fixed per plan; a Growth customer who needs Redshift must move to Scale. ## What can be synced Two kinds of objects can be synced.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: Two kinds of objects can be synced. A cohort sync writes one row per member of a cohort with the columns `distinct_id`, `cohort_id`, `cohort_name`, `joined_at`, and `synced_at`. Both behavioural and static cohorts (see Funnels and Cohorts Specification) can be synced. When a user leaves a behavioural cohort the row is deleted on the next run if the sync is in "mirror" mode, or left in place with `left_at` populated if it is in "append" mode. A metric sync writes the result of a saved KQL query (see SDKs and Kestrel Query Language Reference) with the query's columns plus `bucket_start` and `synced_at`. Metric syncs are subject to the same 10,000-row limit as any KQL query, so a sync that needs more rows should be split by time range or by a breakdown value. ## Scheduling Each sync runs on its own schedule. The minimum interval is 15 minutes; hourly and daily are the most common settings.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: The minimum interval is 15 minutes; hourly and daily are the most common settings. Cohort syncs of behavioural cohorts should not be scheduled more often than hourly because the cohort itself is only recomputed hourly, and running more often just rewrites identical data. A sync can also be triggered manually from the interface or through the API, with manual runs subject to the same 15-minute spacing. ## Idempotency and the 2025-11 incident Since release 4.0.3, every synced row carries an idempotency key composed of `(sync_id, row_hash)`, where `row_hash` is a hash of the row's business columns excluding `synced_at`. The destination table is written with a merge on that key, so re-running a sync, retrying after a network failure, or overlapping two runs cannot produce duplicate rows. This design replaced a position-based deduplication scheme that assumed rows from Kestrel arrived in a stable order.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: This design replaced a position-based deduplication scheme that assumed rows from Kestrel arrived in a stable order. When the Osprey query engine shipped in release 4.0, row ordering for identical queries was no longer guaranteed, and between 2025-11-03 and 2025-11-05 the sync wrote duplicate rows into the Snowflake and BigQuery tables of 41 customers. The incident, tracked as INC-2025-11, is described in its post-mortem. Affected customers received a cleanup script that removed duplicates using the same `row_hash` logic now built into the product. ## Destination setup For Snowflake, Kestrel needs a role with `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` on a dedicated schema. For BigQuery, a service account with the BigQuery Data Editor role on a dedicated dataset. For Redshift, an IAM role assumable by Kestrel with write access to a dedicated schema.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: For Redshift, an IAM role assumable by Kestrel with write access to a dedicated schema. In all cases Kestrel creates and owns the tables it writes to and will not touch tables it did not create. Connection credentials are encrypted at rest and can be rotated from the interface without pausing syncs. ## Failure handling If a run fails, Kestrel retries up to three times with a delay of 5, 15, and 45 minutes. After the third failure the sync is paused and a notification is sent to the project's admin email and, on Growth and Scale plans, recorded in the audit log. A paused sync resumes from the last successful run once re-enabled; no runs are skipped, so a sync paused for a day will backfill each missed window in order. ## Region and data residency A sync runs from the same region as the project.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: A sync runs from the same region as the project. EU-region projects (available since release 4.0 on Growth and Scale) sync from Frankfurt, and customers with EU residency requirements should ensure their warehouse is also hosted in the EU, since Kestrel will connect to whatever destination is configured. ## Limits A project may have at most 50 syncs. A single cohort sync may write at most 2,000,000 rows per run; larger cohorts are synced in chunks across consecutive runs. Warehouse-side costs, such as Snowflake warehouse credits consumed by merges, are the customer's responsibility and are not included in the Kestrel plan price. ## Example Acme Retail syncs the cohort "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" to Snowflake every hour in mirror mode and joins it with their order table to measure recovered revenue from their reminder email campaign.

title: Warehouse Sync Specification
text: Acme Retail syncs the cohort "abandoned checkout in the last 7 days" to Snowflake every hour in mirror mode and joins it with their order table to measure recovered revenue from their reminder email campaign. They also sync a daily KQL metric of unique purchasers by country into the same schema for their finance dashboards.

title: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes
text: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes Released 2025-01-21 to all regions. This is a minor release focused on cohort tooling, funnel analysis depth, and the general availability of the Go SDK. No breaking changes are included, but please read the deprecation note on the legacy ingest endpoint before planning your next SDK upgrade. ## Highlights Cohort CSV upload. You can now create a static cohort by uploading a CSV of user identifiers directly from the Cohorts page. Each upload accepts up to 250,000 user IDs. The file must have a single column named user_id; any additional columns are ignored. Static cohorts created from CSV are not recomputed on a schedule, unlike behavioural cohorts, which continue to refresh every hour. Static cohorts count toward the existing limit of 200 cohorts per project. A common use is importing a list of users from a marketing campaign so you can compare their funnel conversion against everyone else.

title: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes
text: A common use is importing a list of users from a marketing campaign so you can compare their funnel conversion against everyone else. Funnel breakdown raised from 2 to 3 properties. Before 3.4, a funnel report could be broken down by at most two properties, for example country and device type. That ceiling has been raised to three properties, so you can now segment a checkout funnel by country, device type and acquisition channel in one view. Breakdown values are still capped at the 50 most frequent combinations per report; combinations beyond that are grouped into an "Other" bucket. Funnels continue to support up to 12 steps and a conversion window from 1 minute to 90 days. Go SDK general availability. The Go SDK, which had been in public beta since late 2024, is now GA and supported under the standard support policy for your plan.

title: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes
text: The Go SDK, which had been in public beta since late 2024, is now GA and supported under the standard support policy for your plan. It batches events in memory and flushes on a 30-second timer or when 50 events are queued, matching the behaviour of the mobile SDKs. The Go SDK uses the /v2/ingest endpoint exclusively and generates UUIDv7 event_id values by default so that retries are idempotent. ## Smaller improvements The KQL editor now shows the estimated scan range before you run a query, which helps avoid accidentally scanning the full 13-month or 25-month retention window when you only wanted last week. The Beacons list page gained a filter for destination type so you can quickly see which alerts route to Slack versus webhook. The JavaScript SDK now records the page title alongside auto-captured page views.

title: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes
text: The JavaScript SDK now records the page title alongside auto-captured page views. Event property validation errors returned by the ingest API now include the offending property name in the response body, which makes it much easier to find a property value that exceeds the 4 KB limit. ## Deprecation notice The /v1/ingest endpoint is deprecated as of 3.4. It continues to function for now, but it will be removed in a future major release. All current SDKs already use /v2/ingest. If you have a custom integration that still posts to /v1/ingest, migrate it to /v2/ingest, which supports batches of up to 500 events or 2 MB per request, returns HTTP 202 on acceptance, and returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when a project exceeds its ingest rate limit. See the Event Ingestion API specification for the full contract. ## Known issues

title: Kestrel 3.4 Release Notes
text: Uploading a CSV with Windows line endings occasionally produces a trailing empty user ID, which is silently dropped; a fix is scheduled for a patch release. Funnel reports with three breakdown properties and more than eight steps can take noticeably longer to render on projects near the top of the Growth event allowance. There is no change to plan limits in this release; the Starter plan ingest rate limit remains 200 requests per second per project, and Growth remains 1,800 requests per second per project. ## Upgrade notes There is nothing to do for hosted customers; 3.4 is live for everyone. SDK users should upgrade to the latest SDK versions to pick up the page-title capture in JavaScript and the improved validation error messages. Go SDK beta users must update their import path to the GA module path, which is documented in the SDK overview. As always, questions can go to support through the channel included in your plan.

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes Released 2025-04-15. Kestrel 3.5 raises the ingest ceiling for Starter projects, adds a second evaluation mode to Beacons, introduces a shorthand time filter in KQL, and ships an async client in the Python SDK. There are no breaking changes. ## Starter ingest limit raised from 200 to 350 requests per second The most requested change from Starter customers was more headroom on the ingest API during traffic spikes. Effective with 3.5, the Starter plan ingest rate limit is raised from 200 requests per second per project to 350 requests per second per project. Growth remains at 1,800 requests per second and Scale remains at 7,500 requests per second. The limit applies to request count, not event count, so batching multiple events into a single /v2/ingest call (up to 500 events or 2 MB) remains the most effective way to stay under the limit.

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: The limit applies to request count, not event count, so batching multiple events into a single /v2/ingest call (up to 500 events or 2 MB) remains the most effective way to stay under the limit. Requests above the limit still receive HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and all official SDKs honour that header automatically. Note that the monthly event allowance for Starter is unchanged at 2,000,000 events. ## Beacons percentage-change mode Beacons previously supported a single evaluation mode: a fixed threshold on a metric. 3.5 adds a percentage-change mode, which compares the current evaluation window against the same window in the previous period and fires when the change exceeds the configured percentage in either direction. For example, you can now alert when daily sign-ups fall more than 20 percent compared with the previous day.

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: For example, you can now alert when daily sign-ups fall more than 20 percent compared with the previous day. Beacons continue to be evaluated every 5 minutes, and the per-project Beacon limits are unchanged: 5 on Starter, 60 on Growth and 500 on Scale. Destinations remain Slack, webhook and email. ## KQL SINCE shorthand KQL gains a SINCE keyword that accepts relative durations, so a query such as EVENTS WHERE name = 'checkout' SINCE 7d COUNT BY country now works without an explicit timestamp range. Supported units are m for minutes, h for hours and d for days. SINCE is bounded by your plan retention window, so SINCE 400d on a Growth project will be clamped to 13 months. Query limits are unchanged in this release: a maximum of 10,000 rows per query and a 30-second timeout. ## Python SDK async client The Python SDK now includes an asyncio-compatible client alongside the existing synchronous client.

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: The Python SDK now includes an asyncio-compatible client alongside the existing synchronous client. It shares the same batching behaviour, flushing every 30 seconds or when 50 events are queued, and generates UUIDv7 event_id values for idempotent retries. The async client is recommended for FastAPI and other async web frameworks where a blocking flush would stall request handling. ## Smaller improvements The cohort CSV upload bug with Windows line endings noted in the 3.4 release notes is fixed. The funnel builder now remembers the last conversion window you used per project. The Android SDK reduced its default memory footprint for the in-memory event buffer. Ingest validation now rejects events with more than 120 properties with a clear error message rather than silently truncating. ## Known issues

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: Beacons in percentage-change mode can fire spurious alerts during the first period after creation because there is no previous period to compare against; we recommend creating the Beacon and waiting one full period before routing it to a paging destination. The KQL SINCE keyword is not yet supported inside subqueries. ## Upgrade notes The Starter ingest limit increase is applied automatically; no configuration change is required. Python users who want the async client should upgrade to the latest SDK release and import the AsyncKestrelClient class. Everything else in 3.5 is available immediately in the web application. ## A note on batching for Starter customers Several Starter customers who hit the old 200 requests per second ceiling were sending one event per request from browser code. Even with the new 350 requests per second limit, we strongly recommend letting the JavaScript SDK batch for you rather than calling /v2/ingest directly.

title: Kestrel 3.5 Release Notes
text: Even with the new 350 requests per second limit, we strongly recommend letting the JavaScript SDK batch for you rather than calling /v2/ingest directly. A single request may carry up to 500 events, which means a well-batched Starter project can comfortably sustain well over a hundred thousand events per second of burst without approaching the request limit. The limit exists to protect shared infrastructure from request storms, not to constrain event volume, which is governed separately by the monthly allowance and overage pricing described on the Plans, Pricing and Limits page.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes Kestrel 3.6.0 was released on 2025-07-08 and was followed by the 3.6.2 patch release on 2025-07-16. This page covers both. 3.6 is a significant infrastructure release: the event ingest pipeline has been rebuilt on Kafka, Trails gains automatic moment detection, and the Android SDK adds an offline queue. The 3.6.2 patch addresses the ingest incident of 2025-07-14 (INC-2025-07). ## New ingest pipeline on Kafka The ingest path between the /v2/ingest API and storage has been rewritten. Accepted events are now published to a Kafka topic named events.raw with 96 partitions, enriched by a separate service that adds geo and device information, and then written to the hot store and columnar storage by a dedicated writer service. The externally visible contract of /v2/ingest is unchanged: batches of up to 500 events or 2 MB, HTTP 202 on acceptance, HTTP 429 with Retry-After on rate limit, and HTTP 413 for oversized batches.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: The externally visible contract of /v2/ingest is unchanged: batches of up to 500 events or 2 MB, HTTP 202 on acceptance, HTTP 429 with Retry-After on rate limit, and HTTP 413 for oversized batches. The practical benefits are more predictable latency between ingest and queryability, which is now typically under 30 seconds, and better isolation between customers during traffic spikes. The Ingest Pipeline Architecture document describes the design in detail. ## Trails moments Trails now detects "moments" automatically on each user timeline. Moments are patterns that usually indicate friction: rage-clicks (repeated clicks on the same element in a short interval), dead-ends (a page view followed by no further interaction before the session ends) and error bursts (several error events within a minute). Moments are surfaced as markers on the timeline and can be used as a filter when browsing Trails.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: Moments are surfaced as markers on the timeline and can be used as a filter when browsing Trails. To be clear, Trails remains an event timeline, not pixel-level session replay; no DOM recording is performed. Trails availability and sampling are unchanged: 25 percent sampling with 30-day trail retention on Growth, 100 percent sampling with 90-day trail retention on Scale, and not available on Starter. ## Android SDK offline queue The Android SDK now persists its event buffer to local storage when the device is offline and replays it when connectivity returns. The batching rules are the same as before, flushing every 30 seconds or at 50 events. Events replayed after more than 72 hours are still accepted by the ingest API but are flagged late=true, which you can filter on in KQL. ## 3.6.2 patch (2025-07-16) On 2025-07-14 between 09:41 and 12:53 UTC the ingest API in the US region returned HTTP 503 for roughly 38 percent of requests.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: On 2025-07-14 between 09:41 and 12:53 UTC the ingest API in the US region returned HTTP 503 for roughly 38 percent of requests. The root cause was a Kafka consumer group rebalance storm triggered when the new 3.6 ingest workers were rolled out with a session.timeout.ms value of 6 seconds instead of the intended 45 seconds. Clients using official SDKs, which retry on 503, did not lose data. Approximately 2.1 million events from custom clients without retry logic were lost. The 3.6.2 patch corrects the consumer configuration, adds a configuration check to the rollout canary so that a mismatched consumer timeout blocks deployment, and improves the 503 response to include a Retry-After header. A full account is in the INC-2025-07 post-mortem. Version 3.6.1 was an internal build and was never deployed to customers. ## Smaller improvements KQL now supports COUNT DISTINCT on user identifiers. Beacons gained a per-Beacon mute switch.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: Beacons gained a per-Beacon mute switch. The JavaScript SDK reduced its bundle size by around 18 percent. ## Known issues Moment detection is not retroactive; only trails recorded after the 3.6.0 rollout have moments. Late-flagged events replayed by the Android offline queue may appear out of order in Trails until the hourly reorder job runs. ## Upgrade notes No customer action is required for the pipeline change. Custom ingest clients should implement retry with backoff on 503 and honour Retry-After on 429, as the official SDKs do. Android users should upgrade to the latest SDK to gain the offline queue. ## What the pipeline change means for latency Under the previous architecture, the time between an event being accepted and becoming visible in funnels or KQL varied widely, sometimes stretching to several minutes during peak hours because ingestion and enrichment shared a single processing pool.

title: Kestrel 3.6 Release Notes
text: Under the previous architecture, the time between an event being accepted and becoming visible in funnels or KQL varied widely, sometimes stretching to several minutes during peak hours because ingestion and enrichment shared a single processing pool. With the Kafka pipeline, each stage scales independently, and the writer service commits to the ClickHouse hot store in small batches, so events are queryable within about 30 seconds in normal operation. Customers who built dashboards that assume a fixed lag should revisit those assumptions. Enrichment failures, for example an unparseable user agent, no longer block the event; the event is written with the enrichment fields left empty and a warning counter is incremented that is visible on the project health page.

title: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes
text: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes Kestrel 4.0.0 was released on 2025-10-07 and the 4.0.3 patch on 2025-11-06. This page covers both. 4.0 is a major release and includes one breaking change: the legacy /v1/ingest endpoint has been removed. It also introduces the EU region, Beacons anomaly mode, the Osprey query engine and the audit log. ## Breaking change: /v1/ingest removed The /v1/ingest endpoint, deprecated since 3.4, has been removed. Requests to it now return HTTP 410 Gone. All official SDKs have used /v2/ingest since before 3.4, so most customers are unaffected. If you operate a custom integration that still posts to /v1/ingest, you must migrate to /v2/ingest before upgrading any dependency that assumes 4.0 behaviour. The /v2/ingest contract is unchanged: batches up to 500 events or 2 MB, HTTP 202 on accept, HTTP 429 with Retry-After on rate limit, HTTP 413 for oversized batches, idempotency through event_id. ## EU region (Frankfurt)

title: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes
text: Growth and Scale customers can now create projects in an EU region hosted in Frankfurt. Data for an EU project is ingested, stored and queried entirely within that region. The region is chosen at project creation and cannot be changed afterwards; to move an existing project you must create a new EU project and re-point your SDKs. The US region remains hosted in Oregon and remains the default. The EU region is not available on the Starter plan. ## Beacons anomaly mode Beacons gain a third evaluation mode alongside threshold and percentage change. Anomaly mode builds a seasonal baseline from the metric's history and fires when the current value falls outside the expected band. Anomaly mode requires at least 14 days of history for the metric; Beacons created on newer metrics stay in a pending state until enough history exists. Evaluation remains every 5 minutes. ## Osprey query engine Queries are now served by a new columnar engine called Osprey.

title: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes
text: Queries are now served by a new columnar engine called Osprey. Osprey reads the hot store for data up to 7 days old and Parquet files on object storage for older data, and caches results for 10 minutes. Most funnel and cohort reports run two to four times faster than on the previous engine. KQL limits are unchanged at 10,000 rows and a 30-second timeout. ## Audit log Growth and Scale projects now have an audit log recording user sign-ins, permission changes, Beacon and Warehouse Sync configuration changes, and API key creation. Retention of the audit log is 90 days on Growth and 400 days on Scale. The audit log is not available on Starter. ## 4.0.3 patch (2025-11-06) Between 2025-11-03 and 2025-11-05 Warehouse Sync wrote duplicate rows into the destination tables of 41 customers using Snowflake and BigQuery. The issue was detected on 2025-11-04 at 14:20 UTC.

title: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes
text: The issue was detected on 2025-11-04 at 14:20 UTC. The cause was that Osprey returns rows in a different order from the previous engine, and Warehouse Sync relied on row position to deduplicate across runs. The 4.0.3 patch replaces position-based deduplication with an idempotency key composed of the sync identifier and a hash of the row content, so re-running a sync is safe. Affected customers received a cleanup script from support. Full details are in the INC-2025-11 post-mortem. Patches 4.0.1 and 4.0.2 contained internal fixes only. ## Smaller improvements Funnel step definitions can now reference a cohort. The Go SDK adds structured logging hooks. The JavaScript SDK auto-capture can be scoped to specific CSS selectors. ## Upgrade notes Remove any remaining /v1/ingest usage before upgrading custom clients. Warehouse Sync customers on 4.0.0 through 4.0.2 should confirm their destination tables are clean after applying the cleanup script.

title: Kestrel 4.0 Release Notes
text: Warehouse Sync customers on 4.0.0 through 4.0.2 should confirm their destination tables are clean after applying the cleanup script. ## Known issues Anomaly-mode Beacons on metrics with strong weekly seasonality may take longer than 14 days to settle on a stable baseline; we recommend reviewing the first two weeks of alerts before routing them to a paging destination. Osprey's 10-minute result cache means that a report re-run immediately after a bulk backfill may show stale numbers until the cache expires; the report header shows the cache timestamp. Audit log entries are written asynchronously and can lag the underlying action by up to a minute. The EU region does not yet offer the extended retention add-on for Growth; this is planned for a future release.

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes Kestrel 4.1.0 was released on 2026-02-03 and the 4.1.1 patch on 2026-02-24. This page covers both. 4.1 adds Redshift as a Warehouse Sync destination, PagerDuty as a Beacon destination, loose ordering for funnels, and doubles the KQL query timeout. There are no breaking changes. The 4.1.1 patch addresses the Beacon delay incident of 2026-02-19 (INC-2026-02). ## Warehouse Sync to Amazon Redshift Warehouse Sync can now write cohorts and computed metrics to Amazon Redshift, alongside the existing Snowflake and BigQuery destinations. Redshift is available to Scale customers only; Growth customers continue to have Snowflake and BigQuery. The minimum sync schedule remains 15 minutes, and Redshift syncs use the same (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key introduced in 4.0.3, so repeated runs never produce duplicate rows.

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: The minimum sync schedule remains 15 minutes, and Redshift syncs use the same (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key introduced in 4.0.3, so repeated runs never produce duplicate rows. Setting up Redshift requires an IAM role with write access to the target schema, as described in the Warehouse Sync specification. ## Beacons PagerDuty destination Beacons can now route to PagerDuty in addition to Slack, webhook and email. Each Beacon can have multiple destinations, so a common pattern is to send informational alerts to Slack and only threshold breaches on critical metrics to PagerDuty. Beacon limits per project are unchanged: 5 on Starter, 60 on Growth and 500 on Scale. ## Funnel loose ordering Funnels have always required steps to occur in strict sequence. 4.1 adds a loose ordering option where a user counts as converting if they performed all the steps within the conversion window in any order.

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: 4.1 adds a loose ordering option where a user counts as converting if they performed all the steps within the conversion window in any order. Loose ordering is useful for onboarding checklists where users complete tasks in whatever order they prefer. Strict ordering remains the default. Funnels continue to support up to 12 steps, a conversion window from 1 minute to 90 days, and breakdown by up to 3 properties. ## KQL timeout raised from 30 to 60 seconds The KQL query timeout has been raised from 30 seconds to 60 seconds. This was requested by customers on the 25-month Scale retention window who run wide date ranges over Parquet storage. The maximum result size remains 10,000 rows per query. Query API concurrency limits are unchanged: 8 concurrent queries on Starter, 40 on Growth and 160 on Scale. ## 4.1.1 patch (2026-02-24) On 2026-02-19 between 15:02 and 15:49 UTC, Beacon alert delivery was delayed by up to 47 minutes.

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: On 2026-02-19 between 15:02 and 15:49 UTC, Beacon alert delivery was delayed by up to 47 minutes. No alerts were lost; they were delivered late. The cause was clock skew on the Beacon scheduler nodes following an NTP configuration change. The scheduler compared wall-clock time against its schedule and skipped evaluation windows that it believed had already passed. The 4.1.1 patch changes the scheduler to use a monotonic clock and to catch up on any windows it missed, and the NTP configuration is now managed through Terraform rather than by hand. Details are in the INC-2026-02 post-mortem. ## Smaller improvements The iOS SDK now supports Swift structured concurrency for flush calls. The audit log records Warehouse Sync destination changes with the previous and new values. Trails now allow filtering by moment type from the Trails list page. ## Known issues

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: Loose ordering funnels cannot yet be combined with cohort-based step definitions introduced in 4.0. Redshift syncs to serverless workgroups may see slightly higher first-run latency while the workgroup warms up. ## Upgrade notes No action is needed for hosted features. Scale customers wanting Redshift should follow the destination setup guide in the Warehouse Sync specification. Beacon users do not need to change anything for the 4.1.1 scheduler fix. ## Why the timeout was doubled Before 4.1, a KQL query that scanned more than roughly 18 months of Parquet data on a busy Scale project would frequently hit the 30-second timeout, forcing analysts to split queries by quarter and combine the results by hand. Osprey improvements in 4.0 reduced scan time considerably, but the long tail remained.

title: Kestrel 4.1 Release Notes
text: Osprey improvements in 4.0 reduced scan time considerably, but the long tail remained. Raising the limit to 60 seconds resolves the vast majority of those cases without materially increasing load on the query tier, because the concurrency limits per plan still bound the total work in flight. Queries that still exceed 60 seconds return a clear timeout error with a suggestion to narrow the SINCE range or add a filter on event name.

title: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ
text: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ This FAQ covers how Kestrel invoices customers, how overage is calculated, and which add-ons are available. Plan features and limits are documented on the Plans, Pricing and Limits page; this page focuses on money. All invoices are issued in US dollars. ## How is overage calculated? Each plan includes a monthly event allowance: 2,000,000 events on Starter and 25,000,000 on Growth. Events beyond the allowance are charged as overage at $0.90 per 10,000 events on Starter and $0.62 per 10,000 events on Growth. Overage for Scale is negotiated in the agreement. Overage is rounded up to the next 10,000-event block. Overage is invoiced monthly in arrears, so an invoice issued on the first of the month covers the previous month's usage. ## Which events count toward the allowance? An event counts the moment the ingest API accepts it, which is when /v2/ingest returns HTTP 202.

title: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ
text: An event counts the moment the ingest API accepts it, which is when /v2/ingest returns HTTP 202. Events rejected with HTTP 413 or HTTP 429 do not count. Events older than 72 hours are accepted and flagged late=true, and late events still count toward the allowance. Duplicate events that are discarded because they share an event_id with an already accepted event are not counted twice. Events ingested during the 14-day trial count toward the trial's hard cap of 500,000 events rather than a paid allowance. ## Is there a discount for annual billing? Yes. Starter and Growth customers who commit to annual billing receive a 15 percent discount on the plan subscription. The discount does not apply to overage or to add-ons. Annual plans are invoiced in full at the start of the term. Scale agreements are always annual and pricing is quoted individually. ## How does the free trial work?

title: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ
text: New accounts get a 14-day trial with Growth features and a hard cap of 500,000 events. When the cap is reached, ingest returns HTTP 429 until the account is converted to a paid plan. At the end of 14 days, if no plan has been selected, the project becomes read-only for 30 days and is then subject to the Data Retention Policy. Trial accounts are hosted in the US region. ## Can I buy extra seats? Growth includes 15 seats and additional seats cost $19 per seat per month, prorated for partial months. Starter includes 3 seats and cannot be expanded; teams needing more must move to Growth. Scale includes unlimited seats. ## Can I keep data longer? Growth includes 13 months of queryable retention. Growth customers can purchase the extended retention add-on, which adds 12 months for $140 per month, giving 25 months, the same as Scale. The add-on is not available on Starter. Scale retention is 25 months and cannot be extended further through an add-on.

title: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ
text: Scale retention is 25 months and cannot be extended further through an add-on. ## What happens when I downgrade? Downgrades take effect at the start of the next billing period. When moving from Growth to Starter, data older than 30 days becomes unqueryable immediately at the start of the new period and is handled according to the Data Retention Policy. Beacons beyond the Starter limit of 5 are disabled, starting with the most recently created, and Warehouse Sync jobs and Trails are paused. EU region projects cannot be downgraded to Starter because Starter is US-only; they must be migrated to a US project first. Seats beyond 3 lose access and their owners are notified. ## What happens when I upgrade? Upgrades take effect immediately and the difference is prorated on the next invoice.

title: Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ
text: Upgrades take effect immediately and the difference is prorated on the next invoice. Retention expands going forward; historical data beyond the previous window is not recovered, because it may already have been deleted under the retention policy. ## How are SLA credits paid? Only Scale has an uptime SLA. Credits of 10, 25 or 50 percent, depending on the availability tier missed, are applied to the next invoice after a claim is approved. Claims must be submitted within 30 days of the end of the affected month. ## Payment methods Starter and Growth are charged to a card on file. Scale customers may pay by invoice on net-30 terms. Failed card payments are retried three times over 10 days before the project is set to read-only.

title: Plans, Pricing and Limits
text: Plans, Pricing and Limits This page is the canonical reference for Kestrel plans. It reflects pricing effective 2026-02-03. Kestrel is offered in three plans: Starter, Growth and Scale. All prices are in US dollars and are billed monthly unless an annual agreement is in place. See the Billing, Overage and Add-ons FAQ for how overage and discounts work. ## Starter Starter costs $47 per month and includes 2,000,000 events per month. Overage is charged at $0.90 per 10,000 events. Starter includes 3 seats. Queryable event retention is 30 days. The ingest API rate limit is 350 requests per second per project, and the query API allows 8 concurrent queries. Starter projects can have up to 5 Beacons. Warehouse Sync, Trails, SAML SSO, the audit log and the EU data residency region are not available on Starter; Starter projects are hosted in the US region only. There is no uptime SLA. Support is by email with a response target of 2 business days. ## Growth

title: Plans, Pricing and Limits
text: Growth costs $412 per month and includes 25,000,000 events per month. Overage is charged at $0.62 per 10,000 events. Growth includes 15 seats, and additional seats can be purchased. Queryable event retention is 13 months. The ingest API rate limit is 1,800 requests per second per project, and the query API allows 40 concurrent queries. Growth projects can have up to 60 Beacons. Warehouse Sync is included with Snowflake and BigQuery destinations. Trails are included with 25 percent sampling and 30-day trail retention. The audit log is included with 90-day retention. EU data residency in the Frankfurt region is available for Growth projects created since Kestrel 4.0. SAML SSO is not available on Growth. There is no uptime SLA. Support is by email and chat with a response target of 8 business hours. ## Scale Scale pricing is custom and quoted by the sales team; there is no published list price.

title: Plans, Pricing and Limits
text: Scale pricing is custom and quoted by the sales team; there is no published list price. Scale is intended for 250,000,000 or more events per month, and overage terms are negotiated as part of the agreement. Scale includes unlimited seats. Queryable event retention is 25 months. The ingest API rate limit is 7,500 requests per second per project, and the query API allows 160 concurrent queries. Scale projects can have up to 500 Beacons. Warehouse Sync is included with Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift destinations. Trails are included with 100 percent sampling and 90-day trail retention. SAML SSO is included. The audit log is included with 400-day retention. EU data residency in Frankfurt is available. Support is 24x7 with a named customer success manager and a 1-hour response target for P1 issues. ## Scale uptime SLA Scale is the only plan with an uptime SLA. Kestrel commits to 99.93 percent monthly availability for the ingest and query APIs.

title: Plans, Pricing and Limits
text: Kestrel commits to 99.93 percent monthly availability for the ingest and query APIs. If availability in a calendar month falls below 99.93 percent, the customer receives a service credit of 10 percent of that month's fees. If availability falls below 99.5 percent the credit is 25 percent, and below 99.0 percent the credit is 50 percent. Credits are applied to the next invoice and must be requested within 30 days of the end of the affected month. ## Regions All plans can create projects in the US region, hosted in Oregon, which is the default. Growth and Scale can additionally create projects in the EU region, hosted in Frankfurt. The region is fixed at project creation and cannot be changed later. ## Choosing a plan Teams evaluating Kestrel usually start on a 14-day trial, which provides Growth features with a hard cap of 500,000 events.

title: Plans, Pricing and Limits
text: Teams evaluating Kestrel usually start on a 14-day trial, which provides Growth features with a hard cap of 500,000 events. Starter suits small products with a handful of analysts who need funnels and cohorts and can live with 30 days of history. Growth is the typical choice for a product team that wants a year of history, Trails, Beacons at scale and Warehouse Sync. Scale is for organisations that need SSO, an SLA, long retention or Redshift. Contact sales through the account settings page for a Scale quote or to discuss annual agreements on Starter and Growth, which carry a 15 percent discount.

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text: ## Scope This runbook covers production deployment and rollback for all Kestrel services in both regions (US Oregon and EU Frankfurt). It applies to the Ingest API, Enricher, Writer, Osprey, the Beacon scheduler, Warehouse Sync workers, and the web application. Database migrations have their own procedure and are not covered here. ## Deployment model Every service deploys through Argo Rollouts using a blue/green strategy with a progressive canary. A merge to main builds an image, runs the integration suite, and creates a Rollout in the staging cluster. Promotion to production is a manual approval in Argo by the engineer who merged the change, during business hours in their office (Bengaluru or Amsterdam) unless the change is a hotfix approved by the on-call lead. The production canary progresses in three steps: 1. 5 percent of traffic to the new revision, 20-minute soak. 2. 25 percent of traffic, 20-minute soak. 3. 100 percent of traffic.

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text:
100 percent of traffic. The old revision is kept warm for 60 minutes before scale-down so rollback is instant. A full rollout therefore takes a minimum of 40 minutes before reaching 100 percent. Do not shorten the soak steps; the 20-minute window exists because the Beacon evaluator runs every 5 minutes and we want at least four evaluation cycles on the new revision before promoting. ## Automatic rollback Argo analysis templates watch two signals during each soak. If either trips, the rollout aborts and traffic returns to the previous revision without human action: - HTTP 5xx error rate above 0.5 percent, measured over a 5-minute window on the canary pods only.
- p95 request latency above 800 ms, measured the same way. For Osprey the latency metric is osprey.query.p95. An automatic rollback pages the primary on-call and posts to #deploys with the analysis run that failed. ## Consumer configuration canary

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text: After INC-2025-07, in which a v3.6 ingest worker shipped with session.timeout.ms set to 6 seconds instead of 45 seconds and triggered a three-hour rebalance storm, we added a pre-flight check for any service that runs a Kafka consumer. Before the 5 percent step, the pipeline starts one pod of the new revision in a dedicated consumer group against a mirror topic and asserts that its effective consumer configuration matches the values in the Ingest Pipeline Architecture page. A mismatch fails the rollout before any production traffic is affected. The check currently validates session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms, max.poll.interval.ms and max.poll.records. ## Regions The US region always deploys first. The EU region begins its rollout only after US reaches 100 percent and has soaked for 60 minutes. Region-specific rollbacks are allowed; it is normal to roll back EU while US stays on the new revision. ## Manual rollback

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text: If a problem is noticed that the automatic thresholds do not catch, for example wrong data rather than errors, roll back manually: 1. Run kubectl argo rollouts abort <rollout> -n <namespace> in the affected region. This shifts traffic back to the stable revision. 2. Confirm in the Argo dashboard that the stable revision is receiving 100 percent of traffic. 3. Post in #deploys with the rollout name, the reason, and whether the EU region is affected. 4. If the previous revision has already been scaled down (more than 60 minutes after full promotion), use kubectl argo rollouts undo <rollout> to redeploy it. This takes 3 to 5 minutes. 5. Open an incident if customers were affected; the On-call Runbook defines severity levels. For consumer services, a rollback does not replay anything. Events that reached Kafka are safe; the reverted consumers will resume from the committed offsets.

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text: Events that reached Kafka are safe; the reverted consumers will resume from the committed offsets. If a bad revision wrote incorrect data to the hot store, coordinate with the Osprey team on a targeted replay from events.enriched. ## Hotfixes A hotfix is a change that fixes an active incident. Hotfixes skip staging soak but not the production canary, although the on-call lead may reduce each soak to 10 minutes. The three patch releases in the last year (v3.6.2, v4.0.3 and v4.1.1) all used this path. Hotfixes still require a reviewer; the reviewer may be the secondary on-call. ## Feature flags Prefer shipping behind a flag over long-lived branches. Flags are evaluated per project and can be enabled for a percentage of projects, a plan tier, or a list of project IDs. The EU region, anomaly Beacons and loose-ordering funnels all launched behind flags before being defaulted on. ## Checklist before promoting

title: Deployment and Rollback Runbook
text:
- Staging integration suite green.
- Change has a rollback note in the PR description.
- Any new Kafka consumer setting reflected in the Ingest Pipeline Architecture page.
- Migration, if any, already applied and backward compatible with the current revision.
- Status page components identified in case of rollback.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: ## Purpose This page describes the event ingest pipeline as shipped in Kestrel v3.6. It replaces the older single-service ingest path that wrote directly to the hot store. Anyone touching ingest workers, Kafka topics, or the writer should read this before changing configuration. The public contract is documented separately in the Event Ingestion API specification; this page is about what happens after a request is accepted. ## High-level flow Traffic enters through the regional load balancer and is routed to the Ingest API, a Go service that terminates TLS, authenticates the project key, validates the batch, and returns HTTP 202 as soon as the batch has been durably written to Kafka. A batch is at most 500 events or 2 MB; anything larger is rejected with 413 before it reaches the queue. Rate limiting is enforced at this layer per project according to plan (350 requests per second on Starter, 1,800 on Growth, 7,500 on Scale).

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: Rate limiting is enforced at this layer per project according to plan (350 requests per second on Starter, 1,800 on Growth, 7,500 on Scale). Over-limit requests get a 429 with a Retry-After header. Accepted batches are produced to the Kafka topic events.raw, which has 96 partitions. Partition key is the project ID hashed with the user ID, so all events for a given user in a project land on the same partition and preserve relative order. Retention on events.raw is 72 hours, which gives us headroom to replay if a downstream consumer is broken. The Enricher consumer group reads events.raw, resolves geo information from the client IP, parses user-agent strings into device, OS and browser fields, normalises timestamps to UTC, and applies the late-event rule described below. Enriched records are produced to events.enriched, also 96 partitions, same key. The Writer consumer group reads events.enriched and writes to two places.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: The Writer consumer group reads events.enriched and writes to two places. First, it inserts into the ClickHouse hot store, which holds the most recent 7 days and serves the latency-sensitive queries. Second, it accumulates rows into Parquet files that are flushed to object storage every 60 seconds or 64 MB, whichever comes first. Parquet files are partitioned by project, region and day. The Osprey query engine (see Osprey Query Engine Architecture) reads from ClickHouse for the last 7 days and from Parquet for anything older. ## Late events The API accepts events regardless of their client timestamp, but the Enricher marks any event whose timestamp is more than 72 hours before ingestion time with late=true.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: The API accepts events regardless of their client timestamp, but the Enricher marks any event whose timestamp is more than 72 hours before ingestion time with late=true. Late events are still stored and still queryable, but they are excluded from Beacon evaluation and from real-time funnel counts, because retroactively changing a metric that an alert already fired on causes more confusion than it resolves. Mobile SDKs with the offline queue (Android from v3.6) are the main source of late events. ## Idempotency Every event carries an event_id. We recommend UUIDv7 so that IDs sort by time. The Writer keeps a per-partition bloom filter of event IDs seen in the last 24 hours and drops duplicates before they reach ClickHouse. This is best-effort rather than exact: a duplicate arriving more than 24 hours after the original will be stored twice.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text:
This is best-effort rather than exact: a duplicate arriving more than 24 hours after the original will be stored twice. SDK retries never exceed that window, so in practice duplicates come only from customers replaying their own backfills. ## Consumer configuration Both consumer groups run as Kubernetes Deployments with one consumer per pod. The relevant Kafka settings are: - session.timeout.ms = 45000. Consumers that miss heartbeats for 45 seconds are considered dead and trigger a group rebalance.
- heartbeat.interval.ms = 15000.
- max.poll.interval.ms = 300000.
- max.poll.records = 2000 for the Enricher, 5000 for the Writer. The 45-second session timeout was chosen deliberately. During a rolling deploy, pods leave and join the group over several minutes. A short session timeout makes every pod change look like a failure, and a group of 96 partitions across 24 pods can spend more time rebalancing than consuming.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: A short session timeout makes every pod change look like a failure, and a group of 96 partitions across 24 pods can spend more time rebalancing than consuming. This exact failure mode caused INC-2025-07 when a v3.6 worker image shipped with a 6-second timeout; the Deployment and Rollback Runbook now includes a consumer-config canary specifically to catch it. ## Capacity and scaling Each Enricher pod comfortably handles about 25,000 events per second. Writer pods are limited by ClickHouse insert throughput rather than CPU, and we batch inserts to 10,000 rows. Both groups scale horizontally on consumer lag, with a target of under 30 seconds between production to events.raw and availability in the hot store. The p95 for this end-to-end lag in the US region during June 2025 was 11 seconds. Kafka itself runs as a 9-broker cluster per region with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas of 2.

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: Kafka itself runs as a 9-broker cluster per region with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas of 2. The EU region, planned for v4.0, will be a fully separate Kafka cluster and hot store; nothing in this pipeline crosses regions. ## Failure modes to know about If the Ingest API cannot produce to Kafka within 2 seconds, it returns 503 to the client. SDK clients retry with exponential backoff, so a short broker hiccup is invisible to customers. Clients without retry logic lose those events, which is exactly what happened during INC-2025-07.
