If the Writer falls behind, the hot store simply lags; queries return slightly stale data but nothing is lost, because events.raw retains 72 hours. If ClickHouse is unavailable, the Writer continues flushing Parquet and replays the hot-store inserts once ClickHouse returns. The alert ingest.writer.lag_seconds fires at 120 seconds and pages the primary on-call (see On-call Runbook). ## Ownership

title: Ingest Pipeline Architecture
text: Platform Engineering owns the Ingest API, Kafka, Enricher and Writer. Schema changes to enriched events must be reviewed by the Osprey team because they affect the Parquet layout.

title: On-call Runbook
text: ## Rotation Kestrel runs a single engineering on-call rotation covering all production services in all regions. The rotation is weekly and starts on Mondays at 10:00 IST. Each week has a primary and a secondary. The primary is paged first; the secondary is paged if the primary does not acknowledge within 10 minutes, and is also expected to join any SEV-1 within 15 minutes of the page. Engineers join the rotation after three months at the company and after shadowing two shifts. The schedule lives in PagerDuty under the service "Kestrel Production". Swaps are arranged directly between engineers and recorded in PagerDuty; a swap that is only agreed in Slack does not count. ## Compensation Engineers on the rotation receive an on-call stipend of $150 per week for the week they hold primary, and half that for secondary, paid with the following month's salary. The stipend is paid regardless of whether any pages occur.

title: On-call Runbook
text: The stipend is paid regardless of whether any pages occur. Time spent responding to pages outside working hours can be reclaimed as time off in lieu, agreed with the engineer's manager. ## Severity levels SEV-1: a customer-facing outage or data loss. Examples: the Ingest API returning errors for a meaningful fraction of requests, the web application unavailable, Osprey failing queries across projects. Page immediately, wake people up if needed. The status page must be updated within 15 minutes of the page and at least every 30 minutes thereafter until resolved. SEV-2: degraded service with a workaround or partial impact. Examples: Warehouse Sync running late, Beacons delayed, elevated latency without errors, a bug affecting a subset of customers. Page during business hours; outside business hours, page only if the impact is growing. Status page update within 1 hour, then hourly.

title: On-call Runbook
text: Status page update within 1 hour, then hourly. SEV-3: minor impact, cosmetic issue, or a problem affecting a single customer with a workaround. Handle on the next business day. No status page update unless a customer asks. Severity can be raised or lowered during an incident. Lowering requires agreement from the incident commander and a note in the incident channel. ## Responding to a page 1. Acknowledge in PagerDuty within 10 minutes. 2. Open the incident channel that PagerDuty creates automatically (#inc-YYYY-MM-NNN) and post what you know. 3. Declare a severity. If unsure between two levels, pick the higher one. 4. For SEV-1 and SEV-2, assign an incident commander. By default this is the primary; the commander coordinates and does not debug. 5. Update the status page according to the cadence above. Use plain language and name the affected feature, not the internal service. 6. Mitigate first, then diagnose.

title: On-call Runbook
text: Mitigate first, then diagnose. Rolling back the most recent deploy is the default mitigation for anything that started within two hours of a rollout; see the Deployment and Rollback Runbook. 7. When resolved, post a resolution note and schedule the post-mortem within five working days. ## Escalation If the primary and secondary cannot make progress within 30 minutes on a SEV-1, escalate to the Platform Engineering lead. Kafka and storage issues escalate to the infrastructure group; Osprey issues to the query team. Customer communication beyond the status page is owned by Customer Success, who monitor the incident channel and handle direct outreach to Scale customers with a named CSM. ## Status page The public status page has components for Event Ingestion, Query API and Dashboards, Beacons, Warehouse Sync, and Web Application, each per region. Only the on-call and the incident commander have write access.

title: On-call Runbook
text:
Only the on-call and the incident commander have write access. Never mark a component green until the metric that paged has returned to normal for 15 minutes. ## Key dashboards - ingest.writer.lag_seconds: pages at 120 seconds.
- ingest.api.5xx_rate: pages at 1 percent over 5 minutes.
- osprey.query.p95: pages at 2 seconds sustained for 10 minutes.
- beacon.scheduler.delay_seconds: pages at 600 seconds.
- sync.run.failures: pages on 3 consecutive failures for any customer. ## Post-mortems Every SEV-1 and SEV-2 gets a written post-mortem owned by the incident commander and reviewed by the Incident Review Board. Post-mortems are blameless, focus on systems rather than individuals, and must list action items with owners and the release in which each fix ships. SEV-3 incidents get a post-mortem only if the commander thinks one is useful. ## Handover

title: On-call Runbook
text: At the end of the week, the outgoing primary posts a handover in #oncall covering open incidents, anything noisy, and any action items in flight. The incoming primary confirms they have read it.

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text: ## What Osprey is Osprey is the columnar query engine introduced in Kestrel v4.0. It replaces the previous engine, which ran every query against ClickHouse regardless of time range and became the main source of query timeouts for customers on 13-month or 25-month retention. Osprey serves every read path in the product: funnels, cohorts, Trails, Beacon evaluation, Warehouse Sync extraction, and KQL queries from the Query API. ## Hot path and cold path Osprey splits each query on a 7-day boundary. Any part of the requested time range within the last 7 days is served from the ClickHouse hot store, which the Writer populates in near real time (see Ingest Pipeline Architecture). Anything older is served from Parquet files in object storage, partitioned by project, region and day. A query spanning both, for example "last 30 days", is planned as two sub-queries whose partial results are merged in the Osprey coordinator.

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text: A query spanning both, for example "last 30 days", is planned as two sub-queries whose partial results are merged in the Osprey coordinator. The cold path uses a distributed scan over Parquet with predicate pushdown on project, day and event name, so most queries touch a small fraction of the files. Column pruning means a query counting checkout events by country reads only the name, timestamp and country columns. For a Growth project with 25 million events per month, a 13-month cold scan on a single event name typically completes in under 4 seconds. ## Result cache Query results are cached for 10 minutes, keyed by the normalised query plan plus the project ID. The cache lives in a regional Redis cluster. Because the hot path changes continuously, a cache hit on a query that includes the current day may be up to 10 minutes stale. Dashboards show a "last refreshed" timestamp for this reason.

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text:
Dashboards show a "last refreshed" timestamp for this reason. The cache is bypassed when a query is issued with the no_cache flag, which the Beacon evaluator always sets so that alerts are computed on fresh data. ## KQL limits The Kestrel Query Language is compiled to an Osprey plan. Osprey enforces the following limits regardless of how the query was written: - Maximum 10,000 rows returned per query. Larger results must be paginated using cursor tokens.
- Query timeout of 60 seconds (raised from 30 seconds in v4.1). A query hitting the timeout returns a partial-result error rather than partial data.
- Concurrency per project is governed by plan: 8 concurrent queries on Starter, 40 on Growth, 160 on Scale. Additional queries queue for up to 20 seconds and then fail with 429. ## Row ordering Osprey does not guarantee the order of returned rows unless the query includes an explicit ORDER BY.

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text: Osprey does not guarantee the order of returned rows unless the query includes an explicit ORDER BY. The cold path scans Parquet files in parallel and merges partial results as they arrive, so two identical queries can return the same rows in a different order. The previous engine happened to return rows in insertion order because ClickHouse tables were sorted by timestamp, and several internal consumers had come to depend on that accidental behaviour. Warehouse Sync was the most important of these: its deduplication logic compared row positions between runs rather than row contents, which broke immediately after the v4.0 rollout and produced INC-2025-11. Any internal consumer that needs stable ordering must add ORDER BY, or better, key its logic on row content. The fix shipped in v4.0.3 moved Warehouse Sync to a (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key. ## Planner

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text: The planner rewrites KQL into a logical plan, then applies a small set of rules: predicate pushdown, column pruning, split on the 7-day boundary, and cohort inlining (a cohort reference is replaced with a semi-join against the hourly cohort snapshot). Funnels compile to a windowed sequence match with the conversion window as a parameter, up to 12 steps. Loose ordering for funnels, added in v4.1, is implemented as a relaxed sequence match that allows intervening events between steps. ## Storage layout Parquet files use Zstandard compression and a row group size of 128 MB. Each file carries a footer with min/max statistics per column, which the planner uses to skip files entirely. Compaction runs nightly and merges the 60-second Writer flushes into one file per project per day. Until compaction runs, a day may consist of several hundred small files, which is why queries over "today" always go through the hot path instead. ## Observability

title: Osprey Query Engine Architecture
text: Every query emits a trace with the plan, the number of files scanned, bytes read, cache hit or miss, and wall time. The dashboard osprey.query.p95 is the primary latency indicator and is part of the automatic rollback criteria in the Deployment and Rollback Runbook. Queries exceeding 30 seconds are logged with their full plan to a slow-query table that the team reviews weekly. ## Known limitations Osprey cannot join events across projects. It cannot query the raw events.raw topic; only enriched events are stored. Trails on Growth are served from a 25 percent sample, so Osprey's Trails path applies a sampling multiplier that is not applied on Scale, where sampling is 100 percent.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text: ## Summary On 14 July 2025, between 09:41 and 12:53 UTC, the Ingest API in the US region returned HTTP 503 for roughly 38 percent of requests. The incident lasted 3 hours and 12 minutes and was classified SEV-1. The cause was a Kafka consumer group rebalance storm triggered by the rollout of Kestrel v3.6 ingest workers, whose image shipped with session.timeout.ms set to 6 seconds instead of the intended 45 seconds. The fix was released as v3.6.2 on 16 July 2025. The EU region did not exist at the time and was not affected. ## Impact Customers whose SDKs retry on 503 (all official SDKs do) lost no data; their events were delayed and arrived once the pipeline recovered. Customers sending events from custom HTTP integrations without retry logic lost events permanently. We estimate about 2.1 million events lost across 63 projects, based on comparing per-project hourly volumes with the previous week.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text: We estimate about 2.1 million events lost across 63 projects, based on comparing per-project hourly volumes with the previous week. Dashboards and funnels for the affected window undercount accordingly. Beacons that depended on event volume fired spuriously for 17 customers. No stored data was corrupted. ## Timeline (UTC) 09:20 — Rollout of v3.6 ingest workers begins in the US region. The consumer configuration canary did not exist at this time. 09:41 — Canary reaches 25 percent. Enricher consumer group begins repeated rebalances. ingest.api.5xx_rate crosses 1 percent and pages the primary on-call. 09:47 — Primary acknowledges. Initial suspicion is a Kafka broker problem because the rebalance logs are noisy on the broker side. 10:05 — Status page updated: Event Ingestion degraded, US region. 10:20 — Rollout is paused at 25 percent but not aborted, on the theory that the new revision was not the cause.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text: 10:20 — Rollout is paused at 25 percent but not aborted, on the theory that the new revision was not the cause. 10:55 — Secondary on-call notices that the new pods leave and rejoin the group every few seconds. Comparing effective config confirms session.timeout.ms is 6000 on the new image. 11:10 — Rollout aborted; traffic shifts to the v3.5 revision. Rebalances stop within two minutes, but the Ingest API continues returning 503 because the produce path has a backlog of pending acks. 11:40 — Kafka producer buffers drained; 5xx rate drops below 1 percent. 12:53 — 5xx rate stable at baseline for 15 minutes; incident resolved and status page cleared. 16 July, 08:30 — v3.6.2 released with the corrected consumer configuration and a canary check for consumer settings. ## Root cause The v3.6 ingest workers introduced a new Kafka client library.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text: The v3.6 ingest workers introduced a new Kafka client library. The library's default session timeout is 6 seconds and our configuration file, which had previously set the value explicitly, was not carried over during the migration. With 24 pods and 96 partitions, a 6-second session timeout means that ordinary garbage-collection pauses were long enough for the coordinator to consider a consumer dead, triggering a rebalance. Each rebalance stalled every consumer in the group, which caused more missed heartbeats, which triggered more rebalances. While consumers were stalled, the Ingest API's producer buffers filled and it began returning 503 after the 2-second produce timeout. The staging environment did not surface this because it runs 3 pods against a 12-partition topic, where rebalances complete in under a second. ## What went well The alert fired within a minute of impact. Status page communication met the 15-minute target.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text:
Status page communication met the 15-minute target. Once the misconfiguration was identified, mitigation via rollout abort was fast, and the retention on events.raw meant that no enriched data was lost for events that had been accepted. ## What went badly We spent over an hour investigating the brokers instead of the change that had just been deployed. The Deployment and Rollback Runbook says to roll back first when an incident starts within two hours of a rollout, and we did not follow it. Pausing rather than aborting at 10:20 extended the outage by roughly 50 minutes. Staging is not representative of production partition counts. ## Action items - Ship corrected consumer configuration. Done, v3.6.2, 16 July 2025.
- Add a consumer configuration canary to the deploy pipeline that compares effective settings against the documented values before the 5 percent step.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-07: Ingest API 503s during 3.6 rollout
text:
Done, v3.6.2, 16 July 2025.
- Add a consumer configuration canary to the deploy pipeline that compares effective settings against the documented values before the 5 percent step. Done, v3.6.2.
- Document consumer settings in the Ingest Pipeline Architecture page as the source of truth. Done.
- Increase staging events.raw to 96 partitions to match production. Done, 25 July 2025.
- Add "rollback first" as an explicit step in the On-call Runbook response checklist. Done.
- Publish guidance to customers using custom integrations recommending retry with backoff on 503 and 429. Owner: Developer Relations, target August 2025.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text: ## Summary Between 3 November and 5 November 2025, Warehouse Sync wrote duplicate rows into the destination warehouses of 41 customers, across both Snowflake and BigQuery destinations. The problem was detected on 4 November at 14:20 UTC and classified SEV-2. The root cause was the Osprey query engine, introduced in v4.0, no longer returning rows in a stable order, which broke Warehouse Sync's position-based deduplication. The fix shipped in v4.0.3 on 6 November 2025 and replaced position-based deduplication with a content-based idempotency key. ## Impact Affected customers saw between 2 and 9 duplicate copies of some cohort and metric rows in their warehouse tables, depending on how many sync runs occurred between the v4.0 rollout and the fix. Downstream reports built on those tables over-counted. No Kestrel data was affected; the duplication existed only in customer warehouses.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text: No Kestrel data was affected; the duplication existed only in customer warehouses. Because the sync writes to append-only staging tables, no customer data was overwritten or lost. Customers on Starter were not affected because Warehouse Sync is not available on that plan. ## Timeline (UTC) 7 October — v4.0 rolls out with Osprey as the query engine. 7 October to 2 November — Warehouse Sync runs normally. In hindsight, the runs during this period were producing rows in a mostly stable order because the cold path was rarely used for cohort extraction; the hot path still returned insertion order. 3 November, 02:00 — Nightly compaction moves the previous week's data to Parquet. Cohort extraction for customers with long cohort windows now hits the cold path and rows arrive in scan order. 3 November, 02:15 — First sync runs with duplicated rows. No alert fires; sync.run.failures counts failed runs, and these runs succeeded.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text: No alert fires; sync.run.failures counts failed runs, and these runs succeeded. 4 November, 14:20 — A Scale customer's data team reports duplicate rows to their CSM, who escalates to engineering. Incident declared, SEV-2. 4 November, 15:05 — Engineering confirms duplicates in the customer's Snowflake staging table and in two other customers' tables. Warehouse Sync is paused for all customers as a precaution. 4 November, 15:30 — Status page updated: Warehouse Sync degraded, both regions. 4 November, 19:40 — Root cause identified: dedup compares the position of each row against the previous run's snapshot, and Osprey no longer returns rows in a deterministic order. 5 November, 11:00 — Cleanup script written and tested against an internal warehouse. Customers are contacted with the script and instructions. 6 November, 09:15 — v4.0.3 deployed with the (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key. Warehouse Sync resumed.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text: Warehouse Sync resumed. Incident resolved once all 41 customers had run one clean sync. ## Root cause The original Warehouse Sync deduplication was written in 2023 against the previous query engine. It stored a snapshot of the previous run's rows and, on the next run, skipped any row whose index matched a row at the same index in the snapshot. This only works if identical queries return rows in identical order. ClickHouse tables sorted by timestamp gave that property by accident, and nobody documented the dependency. Osprey merges partial results from parallel Parquet scans as they complete, so ordering is nondeterministic unless the query has an ORDER BY clause. The Osprey Query Engine Architecture page states this, but the Warehouse Sync code was not reviewed against it during the v4.0 migration because it did not appear to use the engine's ordering. Detection was slow because the sync runs did not fail.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text: Detection was slow because the sync runs did not fail. Our alerting only covered run failures, not output correctness. ## What went well Pausing all syncs within 45 minutes of the first report prevented further duplication. The append-only staging table design meant recovery was a delete of duplicates rather than a restore. The cleanup script worked for both Snowflake and BigQuery without customer-specific changes. ## What went badly Twenty-six hours passed between the first bad run and detection, and we learned about the problem from a customer rather than from monitoring. The dependency on row ordering was invisible in the code and the migration review. Customer communication for the 38 customers without a named CSM went out by email only on 5 November. ## Action items - Replace position-based deduplication with a (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key.

title: Post-mortem INC-2025-11: Warehouse Sync duplicate rows
text:
- Replace position-based deduplication with a (sync_id, row_hash) idempotency key. Done, v4.0.3, 6 November 2025.
- Add an output-correctness check to Warehouse Sync that compares row counts against the source query and alerts on drift above 1 percent. Done, v4.0.3.
- Add ORDER BY to every internal Osprey consumer that materialises results, and add a lint rule to flag internal queries without one. Done, v4.1.
- Audit other internal consumers of query results (Beacons, exports) for ordering assumptions. Completed 20 November 2025; none found.
- Add a Warehouse Sync component to the status page. Done.
- Define a customer notification template for SEV-2 data-quality incidents so outreach does not wait for a script. Owner: Customer Success, target December 2025.

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text: ## Summary On 19 February 2026, between 15:02 and 15:49 UTC, Beacon alerts were delayed by up to 47 minutes in both regions. No alerts were lost; every alert that should have fired during the window fired late once the scheduler caught up. The incident was classified SEV-3. The cause was clock skew on the Beacon scheduler nodes following a change to NTP configuration, which led the scheduler to skip evaluation windows it believed were already in the past. The fix shipped in v4.1.1 on 24 February 2026. ## Impact Beacons evaluate every 5 minutes. During the 47-minute window, evaluations did not run. When the scheduler recovered, it evaluated all missed windows in sequence and delivered the resulting alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, webhook and email destinations. Customers received alerts with timestamps up to 47 minutes before delivery. For threshold and percentage-change Beacons this was a delay only.

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text: For threshold and percentage-change Beacons this was a delay only. For anomaly Beacons, the late evaluations used the seasonal baseline as of evaluation time rather than window time, which for 6 customers produced one alert each that would not have fired had the evaluation run on schedule. Those customers were contacted individually. Because the Deployment and Rollback Runbook relies on Beacon evaluation cycles during canary soak, one rollout in progress at the time (a web application change) was held at 25 percent for an additional 45 minutes. No customer impact resulted from that. ## Timeline (UTC) 14:30 — Infrastructure applies a change to the NTP configuration on the scheduler node pool, moving from a regional NTP pool to a set of internal time servers. The change is applied by hand as part of a wider migration to internal time servers.

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text: The change is applied by hand as part of a wider migration to internal time servers. 14:31 to 15:00 — The internal time servers are reachable but one of the three has drifted by several minutes. The scheduler nodes gradually converge toward a skewed time. 15:02 — Scheduler nodes now believe the time is roughly 15:50. The scheduler's evaluation loop computes the next window as 15:55, considers the 15:05 to 15:50 windows already elapsed, and marks them skipped. 15:12 — beacon.scheduler.delay_seconds crosses 600 seconds and pages the primary on-call. 15:18 — Primary acknowledges. Scheduler logs show windows being skipped with a reason of "window in past". 15:26 — Node clocks compared against the ingest nodes; skew of 48 minutes confirmed. Infrastructure paged. 15:38 — Bad time server removed from the NTP configuration; scheduler nodes step their clocks back. 15:49 — Scheduler resumes evaluating.

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text: 15:49 — Scheduler resumes evaluating. It has no catch-up logic, so the primary manually re-enqueues the skipped windows. All missed evaluations complete by 16:10. 16:15 — Incident resolved. Status page was not updated, consistent with SEV-3 handling, but a note was posted in the customer changelog the same day. 24 February, 10:00 — v4.1.1 released. ## Root cause The scheduler used wall-clock time to decide which evaluation windows were due and treated any window older than the current wall-clock time as already handled. This was safe as long as the clock only moved forward at a normal rate. The NTP change introduced a fast-forward step of about 48 minutes, and the scheduler dutifully skipped everything in between. When the clock was corrected backwards, the scheduler had already recorded those windows as done.

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text: When the clock was corrected backwards, the scheduler had already recorded those windows as done. The NTP change was applied by hand to a node pool rather than through the Terraform configuration that manages every other node pool, so it did not go through review and was not tested in staging. ## What went well The delay alert fired within 10 minutes of the first skipped window. Diagnosis was quick because the scheduler logs clearly stated why windows were being skipped. The manual re-enqueue recovered every missed window without duplicates, because Beacon deliveries are keyed by window start time. ## What went badly The scheduler had no defence against a clock step, forwards or backwards. Manual infrastructure changes outside Terraform are still possible. Anomaly evaluations for missed windows used the wrong baseline, which the re-enqueue procedure did not account for. ## Action items

title: Post-mortem INC-2026-02: Beacon alert delays
text:
- Switch the scheduler to a monotonic clock for window progression and add automatic catch-up for skipped windows, with a cap of 12 windows (one hour). Done, v4.1.1, 24 February 2026.
- Evaluate catch-up anomaly windows against the baseline as of the window time, not evaluation time. Done, v4.1.1.
- Manage NTP configuration for all node pools through Terraform and block manual edits with a policy check. Done, 23 February 2026.
- Alert on clock skew above 30 seconds between any two node pools. Done, 25 February 2026.
- Add a scheduler chaos test that steps the clock forward and backward in staging before each release. Owner: Platform Engineering, target v4.2.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: ## Purpose and scope This policy defines how long Kestrel Labs keeps customer event data, account data, and operational backups, and what happens to that data when a retention period ends. It applies to every Kestrel project in both the US (Oregon) and EU (Frankfurt) regions, and to all internal systems that hold a copy of customer data, including the hot store, the columnar storage tier, cold storage, and backup snapshots. Version 2 of this policy takes effect on 2025-09-01 and supersedes version 1 in full. Questions should go to the Security & Compliance team; product-facing wording lives in the Product FAQ and the Plans and Limits documentation. ## Queryable retention by plan The primary retention window is set by the customer's plan and is the period during which events are queryable through the Kestrel application, KQL, and the Query API. Starter projects retain 30 days of events.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: Starter projects retain 30 days of events. Growth projects retain 13 months, and Growth customers may purchase the extended retention add-on, which adds a further 12 months. Scale projects retain 25 months. Trails have their own, shorter windows: 30 days on Growth and 90 days on Scale. Audit log entries are retained for 90 days on Growth and 400 days on Scale. These windows are enforced by the Writer service, which tags each Parquet partition with an expiry date when it is written, and by a nightly expiry job that moves partitions past their expiry out of the queryable tier. ## Cold storage after the retention window When a partition leaves the queryable tier it is moved to cold storage rather than deleted immediately. Under version 2 of this policy, raw events are held in cold storage for 30 days after the end of the plan retention window, and are then deleted permanently.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: Under version 2 of this policy, raw events are held in cold storage for 30 days after the end of the plan retention window, and are then deleted permanently. The 30-day cold period exists so that we can recover from an accidental plan downgrade, a billing lapse, or a mistaken project deletion without restoring from backups. During the cold period the data is not queryable by the customer and is not visible in the product. Restores from cold storage are performed only on written request from a project owner and are logged in the audit trail. Cold storage is not a way to keep data beyond the plan window. Customers who need longer queryable history should move to a higher plan or, on Growth, purchase the extended retention add-on. Warehouse Sync is the supported route for keeping computed metrics and cohort membership in a customer-controlled system for as long as the customer wishes. ## Account and project deletion

title: Data Retention Policy
text: When a customer deletes a project, the project is placed in a 14-day soft-deleted state during which an organisation admin can restore it. After 14 days the project's events, cohorts, funnels, Beacons, Warehouse Sync configuration, and API keys are purged from the queryable tier and from cold storage. When an entire account is closed, all data belonging to that account is purged within 14 days of closure. Purge jobs write a completion record that includes the project identifier, the region, and the storage tiers touched; these records are retained for two years for audit purposes and contain no event content. ## Backups Operational backups of the hot store, metadata database, and configuration are taken daily and retained for 35 days. Backups exist for disaster recovery only.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: Backups exist for disaster recovery only. They are encrypted with the same AES-256 keys used for primary storage, are region-local (a Frankfurt project is never backed up to Oregon and vice versa), and are not used to serve customer restore requests. Data that has been purged from primary storage will therefore be absent from backups no later than 35 days after the purge completes. ## Late and flagged events Events that arrive more than 72 hours after their timestamp are accepted by the Ingestion API and flagged as late. Late events are retained according to the same plan window as any other event, calculated from the event timestamp rather than the arrival time. This means a very late event may enter the queryable tier already close to its expiry. ## Changes from v1 Version 1 of this policy, which several older documents still describe, kept raw events in cold storage for 90 days after the plan retention window.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: Version 1 of this policy, which several older documents still describe, kept raw events in cold storage for 90 days after the plan retention window. Effective 2025-09-01 that period is shortened to 30 days. The change reduces our storage footprint and shortens the interval between a customer's retention window ending and the data being permanently gone, which simplifies our answers to data-protection enquiries. No other retention windows changed between v1 and v2. Teams maintaining customer-facing documentation should update any reference to a 90-day cold period; in particular, the Security and Compliance Overview has not yet been revised and should be read in light of this section. ## Exceptions and review Exceptions to this policy require written approval from the head of Security & Compliance and are time-limited to 90 days. Legal holds override this policy for the specific projects named in the hold.

title: Data Retention Policy
text: Legal holds override this policy for the specific projects named in the hold. This policy is reviewed annually, or sooner if a plan structure or storage architecture change makes it inaccurate.

title: Employee Handbook
text: ## Welcome This handbook collects the people policies that apply to everyone employed by Kestrel Labs Pvt. Ltd. It was last revised on 2026-01-05 and applies from that date. Where a local employment contract or the law of the country you work in provides something more generous, that takes precedence. People Operations owns this document; suggestions for changes can be raised with your manager or directly with the People team. ## Offices and working pattern Kestrel Labs has two offices: the headquarters in Bengaluru and a second office in Amsterdam, which opened in March 2025. We work a hybrid pattern. Everyone attached to an office is expected on site two days a week, Tuesday and Thursday, which are the days teams reserve for planning, design reviews, and anything that benefits from being in a room together. The other three days may be worked from home or from the office as you prefer.

title: Employee Handbook
text: The other three days may be worked from home or from the office as you prefer. Fully remote roles exist for some engineering and support positions and are marked as such in the job description; remote employees visit their nearest office for at least one week each quarter, with travel covered by the company. ## Probation New employees serve a probation period of three months. Around the six-week mark your manager will hold a check-in to share feedback and confirm expectations, and at the end of the period you will have a short review. Probation can be extended once, by up to three months, if there are specific areas that need more time; this is always communicated in writing. ## Leave Full-time employees receive 24 days of annual leave per calendar year, in addition to public holidays for the country of employment. Leave accrues monthly and up to five unused days may be carried into the following year, to be used by the end of March.

title: Employee Handbook
text: Leave accrues monthly and up to five unused days may be carried into the following year, to be used by the end of March. Separately, everyone has 12 sick days per year; a medical certificate is requested for absences longer than three consecutive days. Parental leave is 26 weeks at full pay for the primary carer and 8 weeks at full pay for the secondary carer, and can be taken in up to two blocks within the first year. We also offer five days of compassionate leave and paid time off for jury service or equivalent civic duties. ## On-call compensation Engineers who take part in the production on-call rotation receive an on-call stipend of $180 per week for each week they hold the primary or secondary pager, effective 2026-01-01. The stipend is paid through payroll in the month following the rotation and is in addition to normal salary.

title: Employee Handbook
text: The stipend is paid through payroll in the month following the rotation and is in addition to normal salary. If you are paged and work more than four hours outside normal working hours during a rotation, you may take the following working day off in lieu with your manager's agreement. The rotation itself, escalation rules, and severity definitions are described in the On-call Runbook maintained by the platform team; this handbook only governs pay. ## Equipment Every employee is issued a laptop chosen from the current standard list, plus a monitor, keyboard, and headset for their home workspace. Equipment is refreshed every three years or sooner if it fails. A one-time home office allowance of $400 is available in your first three months for a desk or chair. Laptops are managed by the IT team, must remain encrypted and enrolled in device management, and are returned on your last day. ## Expenses

title: Employee Handbook
text: Reasonable business expenses are reimbursed when submitted through the expense tool within 30 days with a receipt. Travel should be booked through the company travel tool where possible. Meals while travelling are reimbursed up to $60 per day. Any single expense above $500, and any software subscription regardless of amount, needs manager approval before purchase. Personal expenses, fines, and upgrades to travel class are not reimbursable. ## Learning and development Each employee has a learning budget of $1,200 per year for courses, books, and conferences. Conference attendance that requires travel counts against this budget unless you are speaking, in which case the company covers it fully. Time spent on approved learning during working hours does not need to be made up. ## Conduct and confidentiality

title: Employee Handbook
text: We expect everyone to treat colleagues, customers, and partners with respect, and we do not tolerate harassment or discrimination of any kind. Concerns can be raised with your manager, with People Operations, or anonymously through the reporting form linked from the internal wiki. Customer data may be accessed only for legitimate work purposes and only through approved tools; the Security and Compliance Overview describes the access controls in place. Information about customers, unreleased products, and company finances is confidential and must not be shared outside the company. ## Leaving Kestrel The notice period is one month for most roles and two months for senior engineering and management roles, as set out in your contract. Unused annual leave is paid out on departure. Your manager and People Operations will run an offboarding checklist covering equipment return, access revocation, and an exit conversation.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: ## Overview This page summarises the security controls, compliance posture, and data-handling practices that apply to the Kestrel platform. It is written for customer security reviewers and for new engineers who need a single starting point. It is maintained by the Security & Compliance team; detailed procedures live in the engineering runbooks and are referenced rather than duplicated here. ## Hosting and network Kestrel runs in a single production region in Oregon, United States. All customer traffic terminates at a load balancer that accepts only TLS 1.2 or higher, with TLS 1.3 preferred. Internal service-to-service traffic within the cluster is also encrypted. Ingest and query workloads are separated into different node pools so that a burst of incoming events cannot starve the query engine of resources.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: Ingest and query workloads are separated into different node pools so that a burst of incoming events cannot starve the query engine of resources. Public endpoints are limited to the Ingestion API, the Query API, and the web application; every other service is reachable only from inside the cluster network. ## Encryption Customer data is encrypted at rest using AES-256. This covers the hot store, the columnar storage tier on object storage, cold storage, and backups. Keys are managed by the cloud provider's key management service and rotated annually, with an emergency rotation procedure documented in the on-call runbook. Data in transit is protected with TLS 1.2 or higher on every external and internal hop. API keys are stored as salted hashes; the plaintext is shown to the customer exactly once at creation. ## Data retention Events are queryable for the period defined by the customer's plan.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: Events are queryable for the period defined by the customer's plan. When an event partition ages out of the plan window it is moved to cold storage, where raw events are kept for 90 days after the end of the retention window and then deleted permanently. Cold storage is not customer-accessible and exists to allow recovery from accidental downgrades or deletions. Deleted projects enter a 14-day soft-deleted state before purge. Daily operational backups are retained for 35 days and are encrypted with the same keys as primary storage. Customers who need longer retention should choose a higher plan rather than rely on cold storage. ## Access control Access to production systems follows least privilege. Engineers receive access through role-based groups tied to their team, and elevated access to customer data requires a time-limited grant approved by an engineering manager and automatically revoked after eight hours.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: Engineers receive access through role-based groups tied to their team, and elevated access to customer data requires a time-limited grant approved by an engineering manager and automatically revoked after eight hours. Every elevated access grant, and every read of customer data through the internal support console, is logged. Access reviews are performed quarterly: each manager confirms the access held by their reports, and any access not confirmed within ten business days is removed. Multi-factor authentication is mandatory for every internal system, including source control, the cloud console, and the internal wiki. ## Compliance programme Kestrel Labs is currently undergoing a SOC 2 Type II audit covering the security, availability, and confidentiality trust criteria. The observation period began in early 2024 and the report is expected in mid-2025.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: The observation period began in early 2024 and the report is expected in mid-2025. Customers who need evidence before then can request the auditor's readiness letter under NDA. We do not currently hold other formal certifications. Our privacy programme is aligned with GDPR principles for customers who send us personal data, and we offer a data processing addendum on request. ## Testing and vulnerability management An external penetration test is performed annually by Halberd Security, covering the web application, both public APIs, and the SDK ingestion path. Findings rated high or critical are remediated within 30 days and retested. Internally, dependency scanning runs on every merge, container images are scanned before deployment, and the platform team reviews scanner output weekly.

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: Internally, dependency scanning runs on every merge, container images are scanned before deployment, and the platform team reviews scanner output weekly. We operate a private bug bounty: researchers who discover a vulnerability can report it to the security team by internal email, and rewards are paid at the team's discretion based on severity and reproducibility. We ask reporters not to access customer data beyond what is needed to demonstrate the issue. ## Incident response Security incidents follow the same severity scale as availability incidents. A confirmed breach of customer data is treated as SEV-1: the on-call engineer pages the security lead, affected customers are notified within 72 hours of confirmation, and a post-mortem is published internally within ten business days. Post-mortems are blameless and focus on the sequence of events and the corrective actions. ## Employee security

title: Security and Compliance Overview
text: All employees complete security awareness training during onboarding and annually thereafter. Laptops are centrally managed, run full-disk encryption, and are enrolled in a device management system that enforces screen lock and OS patch levels. Departing employees have all access revoked on their last working day as part of the offboarding checklist. ## Questions Security questionnaires and requests for the penetration test summary or the SOC 2 readiness letter should be routed to the Security & Compliance team through the customer's account contact.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: ## Who this guide is for This guide walks a new customer from an empty account to a working analytics setup in Kestrel 4.1. It is the same sequence our Customer Success team uses on kick-off calls, so if you follow it you will be in a good position when we speak. It assumes you have signed up and can log in. Trial accounts get 14 days of Growth features with a hard cap of 500,000 events; the cap is not raised for trials, so keep test traffic modest. ## Step 1: Create a project and choose a region A project is the unit that owns events, API keys, and seats. When you create one you choose a region: US, hosted in Oregon, or EU, hosted in Frankfurt. The region determines where your events are stored and processed and cannot be changed after the project is created. If you are unsure, pick the region closest to the majority of your users, and if you have data-residency requirements for European users, choose EU.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: If you are unsure, pick the region closest to the majority of your users, and if you have data-residency requirements for European users, choose EU. Customers who later need both regions create a second project; events are not shared between projects. ## Step 2: Install an SDK Kestrel provides SDKs for JavaScript (browser and Node), iOS in Swift, Android in Kotlin, Python, and Go. Most web customers start with the JavaScript SDK because it auto-captures page views and clicks with no extra code, which gives you data to look at within minutes. The mobile SDKs batch events and send them every 30 seconds or every 50 events, whichever comes first, and the Android SDK keeps an offline queue so events are not lost when the device has no connection. Server-side customers typically use Python or Go and call the Ingestion API through the SDK's batch method.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: Server-side customers typically use Python or Go and call the Ingestion API through the SDK's batch method. Whichever SDK you choose, give each event a stable event_id, ideally a UUIDv7, so that retries never create duplicates. ## Step 3: Verify that events arrive Open the Live Events view in the project. Trigger a few actions in your app and confirm they appear within a few seconds. Check three things: the event names match what you intended, user identifiers are set consistently across platforms, and properties you care about, such as plan or country, are present. Remember that an event may carry at most 120 properties and each property value is limited to 4 KB; events that exceed this are rejected rather than truncated. If you see events tagged as late, their timestamps are more than 72 hours old, which usually means a client clock problem. ## Step 4: Build your first funnel Funnels are the fastest way to get value.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: Funnels are the fastest way to get value. Pick a journey with three to five steps, for example signup started, signup completed, first project created, first event received. Set a conversion window that matches the real behaviour, anywhere from 1 minute to 90 days, and start with strict ordering. Once the funnel shows data, add a breakdown by a property such as acquisition channel; you can break down by up to three properties. Funnels support up to 12 steps, but shorter funnels are easier to act on. ## Step 5: Create your first Beacon A Beacon is an alert rule on a metric. A good first Beacon is a threshold on the volume of a critical event, for example fewer than 100 checkout events in the last hour during business hours. Beacons are evaluated every 5 minutes and can notify Slack, email, a webhook, or PagerDuty.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: Beacons are evaluated every 5 minutes and can notify Slack, email, a webhook, or PagerDuty. Leave anomaly mode for later: it needs 14 days of history before it can build a seasonal baseline, so it will not fire usefully on a brand-new project. Starter projects can have 5 Beacons, Growth 60, and Scale 500. ## Step 6: Invite your team Invite colleagues from the project settings page. Starter includes 3 seats and Growth 15; additional Growth seats cost $19 per seat per month. Give the person who owns your instrumentation the admin role so they can rotate API keys, and give analysts the viewer or editor role. On Scale, SAML single sign-on can be enabled so that seats are managed by your identity provider. ## First-week checklist

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: By the end of your first week we suggest you have: a project in the right region, one SDK sending production traffic, a naming convention for events written down, at least one funnel that someone checks weekly, one Beacon wired to a channel people actually read, and your team invited with sensible roles. Growth and Scale customers should also connect Warehouse Sync so that cohorts and computed metrics land in Snowflake, BigQuery, or, on Scale, Redshift; the minimum sync interval is 15 minutes. ## Things people wish they had known Set up user identification before you invest in cohorts, because cohorts built on anonymous users are hard to interpret. Watch your event volume against your plan in the first month; overage is billed per 10,000 events. If your ingest client receives a 429 response, honour the Retry-After header rather than retrying immediately.

title: Customer Onboarding Guide
text: If your ingest client receives a 429 response, honour the Retry-After header rather than retrying immediately. And if you want a longer queryable history than your plan gives you, talk to us about the extended retention add-on or a higher plan rather than trying to re-send old events.

title: Product FAQ
text: ## About this page These are the questions Customer Success is asked most often, with the answers we give as of Kestrel 4.1. Where a fuller explanation exists we point to the relevant specification or policy. If your question is not here, ask your account contact. ## Plans and billing How does the free trial work? A trial gives you 14 days of Growth features with a hard cap of 500,000 events. The cap is not raised for trials; when the trial ends you choose a plan and the project continues with its data intact. What happens if I go over my included events? Overage is billed per 10,000 events at the rate for your plan: $0.90 on Starter and $0.62 on Growth. Scale overage is negotiated in the contract. We do not stop ingesting when you exceed the included volume. Is there a discount for paying annually? Yes, 15% on Starter and Growth when billed annually. Can I add more seats? On Growth, extra seats cost $19 per seat per month.

title: Product FAQ
text: On Growth, extra seats cost $19 per seat per month. Starter is fixed at 3 seats. Scale seats are unlimited. How long is my data queryable? 30 days on Starter, 13 months on Growth, and 25 months on Scale. Growth customers can add a further 12 months with the extended retention add-on for $140 per month. See the Data Retention Policy for what happens after the window ends. ## Regions and data location Which regions do you offer? US, hosted in Oregon, which is the default, and EU, hosted in Frankfurt, which became available in version 4.0. EU residency is available on Growth and Scale. Can I change my project's region later? No. The region is fixed when the project is created. If you need to move, create a new project in the other region and repoint your SDKs; historical events do not transfer. Do you have an APAC region? Not at the moment, and there is no timeline for one. ## Sending events What happens when I get a 429 response?

title: Product FAQ
text: What happens when I get a 429 response? You have exceeded your project's ingest rate limit, which is 350 requests per second on Starter, 1,800 on Growth, and 7,500 on Scale. The response includes a Retry-After header; wait for that many seconds before retrying. Our SDKs do this automatically with backoff. How big can a batch be? Up to 500 events or 2 MB per request to the Ingestion API. Larger batches receive a 413 response. What are late events? Events whose timestamp is more than 72 hours before they arrive. They are accepted but flagged with late set to true so you can exclude them from time-sensitive reports. The usual cause is a client device with the wrong clock, or a mobile SDK draining its offline queue after a long time without connectivity. Why are my duplicate events not deduplicated? Deduplication relies on the event_id field. If your client generates a new identifier on every retry, we cannot tell the events apart.

title: Product FAQ
text: If your client generates a new identifier on every retry, we cannot tell the events apart. Use a UUIDv7 generated once per event and reused on retry. How many properties can an event have? Up to 120, with each value limited to 4 KB. ## Analysis features How many steps can a funnel have? Twelve, with a conversion window between 1 minute and 90 days, and breakdown by up to 3 properties. Loose ordering, where steps can happen in any order, was added in 4.1. How often are cohorts recomputed? Behavioural cohorts are recomputed hourly. Static cohorts uploaded as CSV are limited to 250,000 user identifiers. A project can have at most 200 cohorts. Is Trails a session replay tool? No. Trails shows a per-user chronological timeline of events with automatically detected moments such as rage-clicks, dead-ends, and error bursts. It does not record the DOM or capture a video of the screen.

title: Product FAQ
text: It does not record the DOM or capture a video of the screen. Trails is available on Growth, with 25% sampling and 30 days of retention, and on Scale, with 100% sampling and 90 days of retention. Why is my anomaly Beacon not firing? Anomaly mode builds a seasonal baseline and needs 14 days of history before it can evaluate. Until then use a threshold or percentage-change rule. All Beacons are evaluated every 5 minutes. Which destinations can a Beacon notify? Slack, email, a webhook, and, since 4.1, PagerDuty. What are the limits on a KQL query? A query returns at most 10,000 rows and times out after 60 seconds. ## Warehouse Sync Which warehouses are supported? Snowflake and BigQuery on Growth and Scale, plus Redshift on Scale since version 4.1. The minimum schedule interval is 15 minutes. Warehouse Sync is not available on Starter. I saw duplicate rows in my warehouse in late 2025; is that fixed? Yes.

title: Product FAQ
text: Yes. Version 4.0.3 introduced an idempotency key on every synced row. Affected customers were contacted and given a cleanup script; the details are in the post-mortem for that incident. ## Product roadmap Is there a mobile app for viewing dashboards? Not planned for 2026. The web application is responsive and works on a phone browser. Will you add more SDK languages? We publish the languages we support on the SDK overview page and announce additions in release notes; we do not pre-announce specific languages. ## Security and support Is my data encrypted? Yes, AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.2 or higher in transit. See the Security and Compliance Overview for the full picture. What support do I get? Starter has email support with a two-business-day response. Growth adds chat with an eight-business-hour response. Scale has 24x7 support, a named customer success manager, and a one-hour response for P1 issues, backed by a 99.93% monthly uptime SLA.
